verdict.summary:
# Deprecation of TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1

## Direct answers

**1. The deprecating RFC is RFC 8996**, *Deprecating TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1* (IETF, part of BCP 195; published 23 March 2021; produced from `draft-ietf-tls-oldversions-deprecate`).

**2. The status it gave the defining RFCs is Historic.** RFC 2246 (TLS 1.0) and RFC 4346 (TLS 1.1) were **moved to Historic status**. The exact wording of the document is: "Accordingly, those documents have been moved to Historic status."

## The defining documents and their new status

| Protocol | Defining RFC | New status assigned by RFC 8996 |
|---|---|---|
| TLS 1.0 | RFC 2246 | Historic |
| TLS 1.1 | RFC 4346 | Historic |
| DTLS 1.0 (related, also deprecated by RFC 8996) | RFC 4347 | Historic |

## Verbatim grounding

From the Abstract of RFC 8996 (identical text on rfc-editor.org `/rfc/rfc8996`, `/info/rfc8996`, and datatracker `/doc/rfc8996/`):

> "This document formally deprecates Transport Layer Security (TLS) versions 1.0 (RFC 2246) and 1.1 (RFC 4346). Accordingly, those documents have been moved to Historic status."

From Section 1 (Introduction):

> "Transport Layer Security (TLS) versions 1.0 [RFC2246] and 1.1 [RFC4346] were superseded by TLS 1.2 [RFC5246] in 2008 ... Therefore, it is timely to further deprecate TLS 1.0, TLS 1.1, and DTLS 1.0. Accordingly, the aforementioned documents have been moved to Historic status."

## Points that are easy to get wrong

- **Two different statuses are in play.** RFC 8996's *own* status is "Internet Best Current Practice" ("This memo documents an Internet Best Current Practice"), and it is part of BCP 195. The status it *assigns* to RFC 2246 and RFC 4346 is **Historic**. The answer to ask 2 is the latter.
- **Deprecation is not withdrawal.** Moving an RFC to Historic changes its status classification in the RFC Editor/IANA records; the document text remains permanently published and citable.
- **"Historic" is distinct from "Obsoleted by".** RFC 2246 and RFC 4346 were already superseded (by RFC 5246 for TLS 1.2, itself superseded by RFC 8446 for TLS 1.3) before RFC 8996 acted; RFC 8996's contribution is the formal deprecation and the status change to Historic.
- **Scope of the status change.** RFC 8996 also deprecates DTLS 1.0 (RFC 4347) but not DTLS 1.2, and notes there is no DTLS 1.1. The quoted text additionally shows RFC 5469 (DES/IDEA cipher suites) moved to Historic because the TLS versions for which its usage is defined are now Historic. The supplied excerpt begins to describe RFC 7507 (version-fallback SCSV) as superseded and "marks it as ...", but the passage is truncated, so the precise status word applied to RFC 7507 is not asserted here.
- **Rationale recorded in the document** (useful if a reader asks *why* Historic rather than merely "discouraged"): TLS 1.0/1.1 mandate older cipher suites (e.g., TLS_DHE_DSS_WITH_3DES_EDE_CBC_SHA is mandatory to implement in TLS 1.0), lack AEAD cipher suites, and depend on SHA-1 for handshake integrity.

## Verification procedure (repeatable)

1. Open `https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8996` and read the Abstract: it names RFC 2246 and RFC 4346 and states they "have been moved to Historic status".
2. Open `https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc2246` and `https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc4346`; the status line for each reads "Historic", with RFC 8996 listed as the document that changed it.
3. Open `https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc8996/` to confirm the document identity: RFC 8996, BCP 195, March 2021, from `draft-ietf-tls-oldversions-deprecate` (the `/history/` page shows the draft-to-RFC progression ending at RFC 8996, 2021-03-23).

## One-line answer

RFC 8996, *Deprecating TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1* (BCP 195, March 2021), deprecated TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 and moved their defining RFCs — RFC 2246 and RFC 4346 — to **Historic** status.

Insurance (OASDI) program limits the amount of earnings subject to taxation for
a given year.  The same annual limit also applies when those earnings are used
in a benefit computation.  This limit changes each year with changes
in the national average wage index.  We call this annual

The OASDI tax rate for wages paid in

Social Security's Old-Age, Survivors, and Disability
Insurance (OASDI) program limits the amount of earnings subject to taxation for
a given year.  The same annual limit also applies when those earnings are used
in a benefit computation.  This limit changes each year with changes
in the national average wage index.  We call this annual
limit the contribution and benefit base.  This amount is also commonly referred
to as the taxable maximum. For earnings in 2027, this base is
$192,300.
The OASDI tax rate for wages paid in
2027 is set by statute at 6.2 percent for employees and employers, each. Thus,
an individual with wages equal to or larger than $192,300 would contribute $11,922.60
to the OASDI program in 2027, and his or her employer would contribute the same
amount. The OASDI tax rate for self-employment income in 2027 is 12.4 percent.

Contribution and Benefit Base Determination
Automatic Determinations
Contribution & Benefit Base
Wage-indexed Amounts
Method for determining the base
The formula for determining the OASDI contribution and benefit base
is set by law. The formula is applicable only if a
cost-of-living increase becomes
effective for December of the year in which a determination of
the base would ordinarily be made.  Because there is a cost-of-living increase for December 2026, the
formula is applicable.  The formula states that the base for any year
Y after 1994 is equal to the 1994 base of $60,600 multiplied by
the ratio of the national average wage index for
year (Y-2) to that for 1992, with the result rounded to the nearest
multiple of $300.  If the result is less than the current base, the base
is not reduced.
Base for 2027
Under the above formula, the base for 2027 shall be the 1994 base of $60,600
multiplied by the ratio of the national average wage index for 2025 to that for
1992, or, if larger, the 2026 base of $184,500.  If the amount so determined
is not a multiple of $300, it is rounded to the nearest multiple of $300.

Other Changes
• The Social Security Wage Base for tax year 2026 is $184,500.
• The employer and employee tax rate for Social Security will be withheld at 6.2 percent (up to
$11,439.00).
• The 2026 Social Security and Medicare coverage threshold for Household wages is $3,000.

• Filing Information Returns Electronically (FIRE) is replaced by Information Returns Intake
System (IRIS).
Beginning tax year 2026/ filing season 2027, the Information Returns Intake System (IRIS) will be
the only intake system for information returns. You are strongly encouraged to complete your IRIS
application for Transmitter Control Code (TCC) and begin transitioning to IRIS to ensure you are
ready for the 2027 filing season. FIRE will not be available for submissions (current, prior year, or
corrections) once the system shuts down in 2026 for end of year. The typical TCC application will
be processed within 45 business days, however, processing times may vary.
• Some editorial changes and corrections for clarification have also been made.

Tax rates and the social security wage base limit. So-
cial security and Medicare taxes have different rates and
only the social security tax has a wage base limit. The
wage base limit is the maximum wage subject to the tax
for the year. Determine the amount of withholding for so-
cial security and Medicare taxes by multiplying each pay-
ment by the employee tax rate.
For 2026, the social security tax rate is 6.2% (amount
withheld) each for the employer and employee (12.4% to-
tal). The social security wage base limit is $184,500. The
tax rate for Medicare is 1.45% (amount withheld) each for
the employee and employer (2.9% total). There is no wage
base limit for Medicare tax; all covered wages are subject
to Medicare tax.

verdict.summary:
ANSWER

The US Social Security contribution and benefit base (the OASDI taxable maximum — the most earnings subject to the Social Security payroll tax) for tax year 2026 is $184,500.

STATUS OF THE FIGURE

This is the final, officially announced 2026 amount, not a projection. SSA published the 2026 wage-indexed amounts in fall 2025 together with the December 2025 cost-of-living adjustment (2.8%). No projection band or caveat is needed.

SOURCE VERIFICATION (four independent official sources, all agreeing)

1. SSA, Contribution and Benefit Base (https://www.ssa.gov/oact/cola/cbb.html) — annual table lists 2025: $176,100 and 2026: $184,500.
2. SSA Publication No. 05-10003, 2026 update (https://www.ssa.gov/pubs/EN-05-10003.pdf) — '6.2% on earnings up to $184,500' for 2026 (vs. $176,100 for 2025) for employees and employers, and '12.4% on earnings up to $184,500' for the self-employed.
3. IRS Publication 15 (Circular E) (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/p15.pdf) — 'The social security wage base limit is $184,500' for 2026; W-2/Form 941 reporting instruction: 'Make sure the social security wage amount for each employee doesn't exceed the annual social security wage base limit ($184,500 for 2026).'
4. SSA Publication No. 42-007, EFW2 Tax Year 2026 (https://www.ssa.gov/employer/efw/26efw2.pdf) — 'The Social Security Wage Base for tax year 2026 is $184,500'; Social Security Wages/Tips must not exceed $184,500; Social Security Tax Withheld must not exceed $11,439.00.

ARITHMETIC AND RULE CONSISTENCY CHECKS

- Maximum employee (or employer) OASDI tax for 2026: $184,500 x 6.2% = $11,439.00 — matches the EFW2 field cap of $11,439.00 exactly.
- Maximum self-employment OASDI tax for 2026: $184,500 x 12.4% = $22,878.00.
- Statutory rounding rule (SSA, Contribution and Benefit Base Determination, https://www.ssa.gov/oact/cola/cbbdet.html): the base for year Y after 1994 = 1994 base of $60,600 x (national average wage index for Y-2 / NAWI for 1992), rounded to the nearest multiple of $300, and never reduced below the current base. $184,500 / $300 = 615 exactly, so $184,500 is a valid rounding outcome. $184,500 > $176,100 (2025 base), so the no-reduction proviso is satisfied.
- 2026 was computed from the 2024 national average wage index of $69,846.57 (per SSA's Detailed Calculator update page), consistent with the Y-2 lag in the formula.

SCOPE / DEFINITIONAL BOUNDARIES (so the number is not misapplied)

- Applies per worker, per year, to OASDI (Social Security) only. It is not a household limit.
- Medicare Hospital Insurance (HI) has had no earnings cap since 1993; all covered wages are subject to the 1.45% employee / 1.45% employer HI tax, plus the additional 0.9% HI tax above the statutory high-income thresholds. Do not apply $184,500 to Medicare.
- Amounts above $184,500 remain subject to Medicare tax and are not subject to OASDI; the base also serves as the cap on earnings counted in a Social Security benefit computation.
- SSA also publishes an 'old-law' contribution and benefit base for 2026 of $137,100; that figure is used only in certain benefit-computation contexts and is NOT the payroll-taxable maximum.
- Do not confuse with the adjacent year: the 2027 base is $192,300 (60,600 x 72,800.33 / 22,935.42 = $192,353.14, rounded to $192,300). The 2026 answer remains $184,500.
- Other 2026 figures announced at the same time, for context only: 2026 is the year the 6.2%/12.4% rates apply up to $184,500; one work credit requires $1,890 in 2026; retirement earnings test limits are $24,480 (under FRA) and $65,160 (year of FRA).

BOTTOM LINE

2026 Social Security contribution and benefit base = $184,500 (USD, per worker per year).

Social Security's Old-Age, Survivors, and Disability
Insurance (OASDI) program limits the amount of earnings subject to taxation for
a given year.  The same annual limit also applies when those earnings are used
in a benefit computation.  This limit changes each year with changes
in the national average wage index.  We call this annual
limit the contribution and benefit base.  This amount is also commonly referred
to as the taxable maximum. For earnings in 2027, this base is
$192,300.
The OASDI tax rate for wages paid in
2027 is set by statute at 6.2 percent for employees and employers, each.

IR-2025-111, Nov. 13, 2025
WASHINGTON — The Internal Revenue Service announced today that the amount individuals can contribute to their 401(k) plans in 2026 has increased to $24,500, up from $23,500 for 2025.
The IRS today also issued technical guidance regarding all cost‑of‑living adjustments affecting dollar limitations for pension plans and other retirement-related items for tax year 2026 in Notice 2025-67 PDF, posted today on IRS.gov.
Highlights of changes for 2026
The annual contribution limit for employees who participate in 401(k), 403(b), governmental 457 plans, and the federal government’s Thrift Savings Plan is increased to $24,500, up from $23,500 for 2025.
The limit on annual contributions to an IRA is increased to $7,500 from $7,000. The IRA catch‑up contribution limit for individuals aged 50 and over was amended under the SECURE 2.0 Act of 2022 (SECURE 2.0) to include an annual cost‑of‑living adjustment is increased to $1,100, up from $1,000 for 2025.

For married couples filing jointly, if the spouse making the IRA contribution is covered by a workplace retirement plan, the phase-out range is increased to between $129,000 and $149,000, up from between $126,000 and $146,000 for 2025.
For an IRA contributor who is not covered by a workplace retirement plan and is married to someone who is covered, the phase-out range is increased to between $242,000 and $252,000, up from between $236,000 and $246,000 for 2025.
For a married individual filing a separate return who is covered by a workplace retirement plan, the phase-out range is not subject to an annual cost-of-living adjustment and remains between $0 and $10,000.
Other phase-out ranges and limitations
The notice also provides limitations for 2026 for Roth IRAs, the Saver’s Credit and SIMPLE retirement accounts.

The amount individuals can generally contribute to their SIMPLE retirement accounts is increased to $17,000, up from $16,500 for 2025. Pursuant to a change made in SECURE 2.0, individuals can contribute a higher amount to certain applicable SIMPLE retirement accounts. For 2026, this higher amount is increased to $18,100, up from $17,600 for 2025.
The catch-up contribution limit that generally applies for employees aged 50 and over who participate in most SIMPLE plans is increased to $4,000, up from $3,500 for 2025. Under a change made in SECURE 2.0, a different catch-up limit applies for employees aged 50 and over who participate in certain applicable SIMPLE plans, which remains $3,850. Under a change made in SECURE 2.0, a higher catch-up contribution limit applies for employees aged 60, 61, 62 and 63 who participate in SIMPLE plans, which remains $5,250.
Details on these and other retirement-related cost-of-living adjustments for 2026 are in Notice 2025-67, available on IRS.gov.

Basic elective deferral limit
The basic limit on elective deferrals is $24,500 in 2026, $23,500 in 2025, $23,000 in 2024 and $22,500 in 2023, or 100% of the employee's compensation, whichever is less. The elective deferral limit for SIMPLE plans is 100% of compensation or $17,000 in 2026, $16,500 in 2025, $16,000 in 2024, and $15,500 in 2023. Catch-up contributions may also be allowed if the employee is age 50 or older.
If the employee's total contributions exceed the deferral limit, the difference is included in the employee's gross income.
Time for depositing elective deferrals
Employers must deposit employee contributions to the retirement plan's trust or individual accounts as soon as they can reasonably be segregated from the employer's general assets. The Department of Labor provides a 7-business-day safe harbor rule for employee contributions to plans with fewer than 100 participants.

Employer matching contributions. Tax on excess IRA contributions
An excess IRA contribution occurs if you:
Contribute more than the contribution limit.
Make a regular IRA contribution for 2019, or earlier, to a traditional IRA at age 70½ or older.
Make an improper rollover contribution to an IRA.
Excess contributions are taxed at 6% per year for each year the excess amounts remain in the IRA. The tax can't be more than 6% of the combined value of all your IRAs as of the end of the tax year.
To avoid the 6% tax on excess contributions, you must withdraw:
the excess contributions from your IRA by the due date of your individual income tax return (including extensions); and
any income earned on the excess contribution.
See Publication 590-A for certain conditions that may allow you to avoid including withdrawals of excess contributions in your gross income.

verdict.summary:
# 2026 401(k) Elective Deferral Limit (IRC §402(g)) — HR/Benefits Determination

## Answer

**$24,500** — the limit on an employee's elective deferrals to a 401(k) plan for calendar year 2026, before any catch-up contribution.

This is the basic elective deferral limit under IRC §402(g)(1), as cost-of-living-adjusted for 2026. It is up from $23,500 in 2025 (an increase of $1,000).

**Authority:** IRS Notice 2025-67 (2026 cost-of-living adjustments for pension plans and retirement-related items) and IRS News Release IR-2025-111, issued November 13, 2025. The figure is final and officially published — it is not a projection.

Notice 2025-67, verbatim: "The limitation under section 402(g)(1) on the exclusion for elective deferrals described in section 402(g)(3), which includes elective deferrals made to the Thrift Savings Plan, is increased from $23,500 to $24,500."

IRS "Retirement topics — 401(k) and profit-sharing plan contribution limits," verbatim: "The limit on employee elective deferrals (for traditional and safe harbor plans) is: $24,500 in 2026, subject to cost-of-living adjustments."

## Scope of the figure

**What counts against the $24,500:**
- The employee's own salary-reduction contributions — pre-tax (traditional) and designated Roth contributions alike. Pre-tax and Roth deferrals share this single limit; electing Roth does not create extra room.
- Deferrals to 401(k) plans, and the same dollar limit applies to 403(b) plans, governmental 457(b) plans, and the federal Thrift Savings Plan.
- Aggregation: an employee who participates in more than one plan subject to §402(g) aggregates all elective deferrals across those plans for the calendar year to test against the limit.

**What does NOT count against the $24,500:**
- Catch-up contributions (excluded by the question; see below).
- Employer matching contributions and employer nonelective/profit-sharing contributions — those are tested against the separate §415(c) annual additions limit.
- Rollovers and loan proceeds.

**Two qualifications on the limit — both must be communicated with the number:**
1. The statutory limit is the lesser of $24,500 **or 100% of the employee's compensation** for the year.
2. $24,500 is the IRS ceiling, not a guarantee. The plan document may impose a lower cap, and nondiscrimination testing (ADP/ACP) may force a lower effective limit for highly compensated employees mid-year. For HCEs, the operative number is frequently below $24,500.

## Related 2026 limits — do not confuse with the above

| Item | Authority | 2026 | 2025 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Elective deferrals (the answer) | §402(g)(1) | **$24,500** | $23,500 |
| Catch-up, age 50+ | §414(v)(2)(B)(i) | $8,000 | $7,500 |
| Catch-up, ages 60–63 (SECURE 2.0) | §414(v)(2)(E)(i) | $11,250 | $11,250 |
| Total annual additions (deferrals + employer money) | §415(c) | $72,000 | $70,000 |
| Annual compensation limit | §401(a)(17) | $360,000 | $350,000 |
| HCE compensation threshold | §414(q) | $160,000 | $160,000 |
| IRA contribution limit | §219 | $7,500 | $7,000 |
| IRA catch-up, age 50+ | §219 | $1,100 | $1,000 |
| SIMPLE plan deferrals | §408(p) | $17,000 | $16,500 |
| SIMPLE 401(k) deferrals | §401(k)(11) | $17,000 | $16,500 |
| SIMPLE catch-up, age 50+ | §414(v)(2)(B)(ii) | $4,000 | $3,500 |
| SIMPLE catch-up, ages 60–63 | §414(v)(2)(E)(ii) | $5,250 | $5,250 |
| 457(b) elective deferrals (state/local, tax-exempt) | §457(e)(15) | $24,500 | $23,500 |

Note the hierarchy: catch-up amounts are added **on top of** the $24,500, so a participant aged 50+ in 2026 may defer up to $24,500 + $8,000 = $32,500 (ages 60–63: $24,500 + $11,250 = $35,750), subject to the §415(c) aggregate once catch-up is excluded from that test. SIMPLE plan figures are a different plan type and do not apply to a 401(k).

## Prior-year series (for payroll configuration and communications)

| Year | §402(g) elective deferral limit |
|---|---|
| 2023 | $22,500 |
| 2024 | $23,000 |
| 2025 | $23,500 |
| 2026 | **$24,500** |

## Implementation notes for HR / payroll

1. **Set the 2026 deferral cap in payroll to $24,500**, effective for the first pay date in the 2026 calendar year, and reset per-employee YTD deferral accumulators at that point. The §402(g) limit operates on a **calendar-year** basis regardless of whether the plan has a non-calendar plan year — a fiscal plan year beginning mid-2026 does not shift or prorate the figure.
2. **Test pre-tax and Roth in a single accumulator.** Do not configure separate caps; the $24,500 is a combined ceiling.
3. **Do not reduce the $24,500 by employer match or profit sharing.** Those count only against §415(c) ($72,000).
4. **Catch-up is a separate accumulator**, enabled only for participants who attain age 50 by the end of 2026 ($8,000) and, separately, those who attain age 60, 61, 62, or 63 during 2026 ($11,250 in lieu of $8,000). Catch-up capacity is not available until the base $24,500 (or the plan's lower cap, if the plan so provides) is exhausted.
5. **Excess deferrals:** amounts above $24,500 that are not catch-up are includible in the employee's gross income. To avoid double taxation, excess deferrals (plus attributable earnings) must be distributed by April 15 of the following year under §402(g)(2); excess deferrals corrected after that date are taxed twice. Payroll should flag any participant projected to exceed $24,500 before the final payroll of the year.
6. **Plan-document check:** confirm the plan's own deferral cap (often stated as a percentage of compensation) does not bind below $24,500, and confirm the plan permits catch-up if you intend to communicate the $32,500 / $35,750 combined figures.
7. **Non-calendar plan years:** the §402(g) limit is applied per calendar year for the individual, so a short or fiscal plan year requires allocating deferrals to the calendar year in which they were actually deferred.

## Source verification

- IRS News Release IR-2025-111, Nov. 13, 2025: "The annual contribution limit for employees who participate in 401(k), 403(b), governmental 457 plans, and the federal government's Thrift Savings Plan is increased to $24,500, up from $23,500 for 2025."
- IRS Notice 2025-67, §402(g)(1) paragraph: increased from $23,500 to $24,500.
- IRS Retirement Topics — 401(k) and Profit-Sharing Plan Contribution Limits: "$24,500 in 2026."
- IRS COLA table, "401(k), 403(b), profit-sharing plans, etc." — Elective deferrals: 24,500 (2026), 23,500 (2025), 23,000 (2024), 22,500 (2023).

All four sources agree on $24,500; there is no conflicting figure in the record.

## Out of scope / caveats

- This is the **federal** limit. State tax treatment of deferrals is not addressed.
- This is the statutory ceiling, not advice on an individual's optimal deferral amount or on the SECURE 2.0 Roth catch-up wage threshold (which determines *how* catch-up must be made for higher earners, not *how much* may be deferred) — route those questions to tax counsel or the plan's recordkeeper.
- If the question was intended for a non-401(k) plan type (SIMPLE, 403(b), 457(b)), the applicable figure differs in some cases; the table above covers the common alternatives.

§ 50.20 National primary ambient air quality standards for PM2.5.




(a) The national primary ambient air quality standards for PM2.5 are 9.0 micrograms per cubic meter (µg/m3) annual arithmetic mean concentration and 35 µg/m3 24-hour average concentration measured in the ambient air as PM2.5 (particles with an aerodynamic diameter less than or equal to a nominal 2.5 micrometers) by either:

(132.6 KB)
On February 7, 2024, EPA strengthened the National Ambient Air Quality Standards for Particulate Matter (PM NAAQS) to protect millions of Americans from harmful and costly health impacts, such as heart attacks and premature death. ​Particle or soot pollution is one of the most dangerous forms of air pollution, and an extensive body of science links it to a range of serious and sometimes deadly illnesses. ​ EPA is setting the level of the primary (health-based) annual PM2.5 standard at 9.0 micrograms per cubic meter to provide increased public health protection, consistent with the available health science.
EPA is not changing the current:
primary and secondary (welfare-based) 24-hour PM2.5 standards,
secondary annual PM2.5 standard, and
primary and secondary PM10 standards.
EPA is also revising the Air Quality Index to improve public communications about the risks from PM2.5 exposures and making changes to the monitoring network to enhance protection of air quality in communities overburdened by air pollution.

verdict.summary:
# Current US National Primary (Health-Based) NAAQS for PM2.5

## Answer

| Ask | Standard | Level | Form (how compliance is judged) | CFR cite |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Primary **annual** PM2.5 | **9.0 µg/m³** | Annual arithmetic mean concentration, averaged over 3 years, compared to the level rounded to one decimal place | 40 CFR 50.20(a), (b) |
| 2 | Primary **24-hour** PM2.5 | **35 µg/m³** | 98th percentile of 24-hour concentrations, averaged over 3 years, compared to the level rounded to an integer | 40 CFR 50.20(a), (c) |

Units: micrograms per cubic meter of ambient air (µg/m³), measured as PM2.5 (particles with aerodynamic diameter ≤ 2.5 µm nominal).

## Governing text (current eCFR, 40 CFR 50.20)

> § 50.20 National primary ambient air quality standards for PM2.5.
> (a) The national primary ambient air quality standards for PM2.5 are **9.0 micrograms per cubic meter (µg/m3) annual arithmetic mean concentration** and **35 µg/m3 24-hour average concentration** measured in the ambient air as PM2.5 ...
> (b) The primary annual PM2.5 standard is met when the annual arithmetic mean concentration, as determined in accordance with appendix N to this part, is less than or equal to **9.0 µg/m3**.
> (c) The primary 24-hour PM2.5 standard is met when the 98th percentile 24-hour concentration, as determined in accordance with appendix N to this part, is less than or equal to **35 µg/m3**.
> [89 FR 16380, Mar. 6, 2024]

## Provenance and corroboration

1. **eCFR, 40 CFR 50.20** (fetched 2026-11-16): states 9.0 µg/m³ annual and 35 µg/m³ 24-hour, with source note [89 FR 16380, Mar. 6, 2024]. This is the operative codified text.
2. **EPA, "National Ambient Air Quality Standards (NAAQS) for PM"**: "EPA is setting the level of the primary (health-based) annual PM2.5 standard at 9.0 micrograms per cubic meter... EPA is not changing the current: primary and secondary (welfare-based) 24-hour PM2.5 standards, secondary annual PM2.5 standard, and primary and secondary PM10 standards."
3. **EPA, Timeline of PM NAAQS**, entry for 2024 / 89 FR 16202, March 6, 2024: "Primary | PM2.5 | 1 year | 9.0 µg/m3 | Annual arithmetic mean, averaged over 3 years ... All other primary and secondary PM2.5 and PM10 standards, retained without revision."
4. **CFR 2024 volume PDF** (govinfo) independently shows § 50.20(a) beginning "...are 9.0 micrograms per cubic meter (µg/m3) an-" and § 50.20(c) "...is less than or equal to 35 µg/m3. [89 FR 16380, Mar. 6, 2024]".

Three independent sources agree on both numbers, so neither ask is blocked.

## What the current levels are NOT (superseded values — do not use)

| Value | Where it comes from | Status |
|---|---|---|
| 12.0 µg/m³ annual | 40 CFR 50.18; 78 FR 3277 (Jan. 15, 2013); reaffirmed 2020 (85 FR 82684) | **Superseded** by the 2024 rule. Still physically present in the CFR as § 50.18 but no longer the operative primary annual standard; the 2024 rule relocated/restated the PM2.5 primary standards at § 50.20 with the 9.0 level. |
| 15.0 µg/m³ annual | 1997 review (62 FR 38652) | Superseded (2012). |
| 65 µg/m³ 24-hour | 1997 review | Superseded (2012). |
| 35 µg/m³ 24-hour | 2012 review (78 FR 3085); retained 2020; retained 2024 | **Current.** Unchanged since 2012. |

The single most common error on this question is quoting 12.0 µg/m³ for the annual level; that was correct from 2013 until the 2024 rule and is no longer correct.

## Rounding / statement conventions (so the numbers are stated correctly)

EPA defines the levels asymmetrically, and the answer above follows that:
- **Annual level is expressed to one decimal place** (9.0, not 9). A 3-year average annual mean of 9.04 µg/m³ rounds to 9.0 and meets the standard; 9.05 rounds to 9.1 and violates it.
- **24-hour level is expressed as an integer** (35, not 35.0). A 3-year average 98th percentile of 35.49 µg/m³ rounds to 35 and meets the standard; 35.50 rounds to 36 and violates it.
- Reference/equivalence: measurements must be by an FRM based on 40 CFR part 50 appendix L, or an FEM designated under 40 CFR part 53.

## Scope notes

- **Primary vs secondary.** The figures above are the *primary* (health-based) standards, as asked. For completeness: the secondary (welfare-based) annual PM2.5 standard is 15.0 µg/m³ and the secondary 24-hour PM2.5 standard is 35 µg/m³ — both retained without revision in the December 27, 2024 secondary-standards rule (89 FR 105692). These are *not* the answer to the question as posed and should not be substituted.
- **As-of date.** The answer reflects the standards in force as of the eCFR snapshot fetched 2026-11-16, i.e., post-2024-revision.
- **Pending activity (caveat, not a change).** The EPA PM NAAQS page carries a 03/12/2025 alert: "Trump EPA Announces Path Forward on National Air Quality Standards for Particulate Matter (PM2.5) to Aid Manufacturing, Small Businesses." That is an announced path forward, not a final rule; no fetched source shows a promulgated change to the 9.0 or 35 levels, and the codified text still reads 9.0 / 35. Anyone relying on this answer for a regulatory determination should re-check 40 CFR 50.20 for a subsequent Federal Register amendment before acting.

## Bottom line

- **Annual primary PM2.5 standard: 9.0 µg/m³** (annual arithmetic mean, 3-year average).
- **24-hour primary PM2.5 standard: 35 µg/m³** (98th percentile, 3-year average).

verdict.summary:
ANSWER: 4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level.

1. Governing rule. Under federal OSHA general industry, 29 CFR 1910.28(b)(15) — Walking-working surfaces not otherwise addressed — requires the employer to ensure each employee on a walking-working surface 4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level is protected from falling by guardrail systems, safety net systems, or personal fall protection systems. The general rule in 29 CFR 1910.28(b)(1)(i) uses the same 4-foot (1.2 m) trigger for a walking-working surface with an unprotected side or edge. At exactly 4 feet, protection is required; below 4 feet, the general walking-working-surface rule does not trigger, although other provisions (for example, holes and dangerous equipment) may still require guarding.

2. What counts as protection. Acceptable protection includes guardrail systems, safety net systems, and personal fall protection systems such as personal fall arrest, travel restraint, or positioning systems. Where the standard permits, designated areas may also be used. Equipment must meet 29 CFR 1910.29, and exposed employees must be trained under 29 CFR 1910.30.

3. Measurement. The 4 feet is the vertical distance from the walking-working surface on which the employee stands or works to the lower level. It is not the height of the guardrail. Guardrail height is separately addressed in 1910.29(b), which requires the top rail to be 42 inches (107 cm) plus or minus 3 inches (8 cm) above the walking-working surface.

4. Surface-specific provisions using the same 4-foot trigger. The following do not change the answer; they confirm the 4-foot baseline:
- Hoist areas: 1910.28(b)(2), 4 feet or more.
- Holes: 1910.28(b)(3), 4 feet or more; holes less than 4 feet above a lower level must still be protected by covers or guardrails to prevent tripping or stepping into them.
- Stairway landings: 1910.28(b)(11), unprotected side or edge 4 feet or more.
- Rope descent systems: 1910.28(b)(12), 4 feet or more.
- Slaughtering facility platforms: 1910.28(b)(14), 4 feet or more.

5. Provisions that are not a different height threshold. Do not confuse these with the general height answer:
- Dangerous equipment, 1910.28(b)(6): protection is required for employees less than 4 feet above dangerous equipment and for employees 4 feet or more above it, with different permitted means. This is an equipment-hazard rule, not a different general walking-working-surface height.
- Openings, 1910.28(b)(7): the rule is keyed to an inside bottom edge less than 39 inches (99 cm) above the walking-working surface and an outside bottom edge 4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level.
- Low-slope roofs, 1910.28(b)(13): the rule is keyed to distance from the roof edge — less than 6 feet, at least 6 feet but less than 15 feet, and 15 feet or more — not to a 6-foot height. The 6 feet and 15 feet figures are distances, not height thresholds.

6. Scope and jurisdiction. This is the federal OSHA general-industry baseline under 29 CFR Part 1910, Subpart D. Construction work is governed by 29 CFR 1926.501(b)(1), which uses 6 feet; that is not the general-industry answer and is outside the question. OSHA-approved state plans may adopt stricter or additional requirements, so verify the applicable state plan if the workplace is in a state-plan jurisdiction. Maritime and other industry-specific standards are outside this answer.

7. Practical compliance procedure.
(a) Confirm the work is general industry, not construction or another industry-specific standard.
(b) Identify the walking-working surface, the unprotected side or edge, and the lower level.
(c) Measure the vertical distance to the lower level.
(d) If the distance is 4 feet (1.2 m) or more, select and install a guardrail system, safety net system, or personal fall protection system meeting 1910.29.
(e) If the employer can demonstrate that a required system is infeasible or creates a greater hazard, implement the fall protection plan permitted by 1910.28(b)(1)(ii) and 1910.29(k).
(f) Train exposed employees under 1910.30.
(g) Inspect and maintain the walking-working surface and fall protection equipment under 1910.22(d) and 1910.29.

8. Bottom line. The height is 4 feet (1.2 m) above a lower level.

verdict.summary:
# VFR Reserve Fuel Requirement — US-Registered Helicopter (14 CFR Part 91)

## 1. Answer

**20 minutes of flight at normal cruising speed, measured from the first point of intended landing.**

That is the whole of the federal minimum reserve for a helicopter beginning a VFR flight in the United States. It is a *time* requirement, not a volume or weight; the pilot converts it to gallons/pounds using the helicopter's normal cruise fuel burn.

## 2. Governing regulation (verbatim)

14 CFR § 91.151 — *Fuel requirements for flight in VFR conditions*:

> (b) No person may begin a flight in a rotorcraft under VFR conditions unless (considering wind and forecast weather conditions) there is enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and, assuming normal cruising speed, to fly after that for at least 20 minutes.

(Source: eCFR, current as of fetch 2026-11-16; identical text in the GovInfo CFR-2026-title14-vol2 PDF and the eCFR Part 91 page.)

## 3. How the requirement decomposes

The rule has exactly two fuel components:

| Component | What it covers | Wind allowance |
|---|---|---|
| Trip fuel | Takeoff → first point of intended landing | Yes — "considering wind and forecast weather conditions" |
| **Reserve** | **20 minutes after the first point of intended landing** | **No — computed "assuming normal cruising speed"** |

Total fuel required at brake release = trip fuel (wind/forecast-adjusted) + 20-minute reserve.

Key consequences that follow directly from the text:

- **No day/night difference.** Unlike airplanes, rotorcraft get a single figure. Night does not raise it to 45 minutes. This is the single most common error made by pilots transitioning from airplanes.
- **No wind credit on the reserve.** Only the trip leg gets the wind/forecast adjustment. The 20 minutes is flown at the book normal cruising speed.
- **The reserve is measured from the first point of intended landing**, not from the destination of the last leg. On a multi-leg flight, § 91.151(b) is tested at the *beginning* of the flight; each subsequent takeoff is a new "begin a flight" and must independently satisfy the rule.
- **It is a minimum, not a target.** Company minimums, Part 135 OpSpecs, insurance requirements, or pilot judgment may be higher. The regulation sets the floor only.

## 4. Converting 20 minutes into fuel quantity

Reserve fuel = (normal cruise burn rate per hour) × (20 / 60) = burn rate ÷ 3

Use *usable* fuel and the burn rate at the power setting/speed the flight will actually be flown at in cruise.

**Worked example A — piston helicopter, avgas:**
- Normal cruise burn: 16.0 gal/h usable
- Reserve: 16.0 ÷ 3 = **5.33 gal** (≈ 32 lb at 6.0 lb/gal)

**Worked example B — turbine helicopter, Jet A:**
- Normal cruise burn: 200 lb/h (≈ 30 gal/h)
- Reserve: 200 ÷ 3 = **66.7 lb**; at 6.7 lb/gal → **≈ 9.95 gal**

**Worked example C — full flight total:**
- Trip: 1.5 h at 16.0 gal/h, adjusted for forecast wind → 24.0 gal
- Reserve: 5.33 gal
- Minimum fuel at start: 24.0 + 5.33 = **29.3 gal usable**

## 5. Contrasts that are *not* the answer (stated to prevent misapplication)

| Situation | Reserve | Rule |
|---|---|---|
| Airplane, VFR, day | 30 min | 91.151(a)(1) |
| Airplane, VFR, night | 45 min | 91.151(a)(2) |
| **Rotorcraft, VFR, day or night** | **20 min** | **91.151(b)** |
| Any aircraft, IFR (Part 91) | 45 min after the alternate (plus alternate fuel) | 91.167 |
| Helicopter, VFR, Part 135 | 20 min (verify against the current OpSpecs for the certificate) | 135.209(b) |

The 20-minute figure applies to both aeroplanes-with-rotors categories (normal and transport category rotorcraft) and is independent of whether the flight is conducted by day or at night.

## 6. Points from the request that do *not* change the answer

- **FAA-approved Rotorcraft Flight Manual vs. non-approved RFM.** § 91.151(b) contains no RFM condition. The RFM's approval status affects compliance with other operating limitations (e.g., § 91.9(a) and the aircraft's approved operating limitations) and the availability of certain operating rules, but it does not change the 20-minute VFR reserve.
- **Day vs. night.** No effect for rotorcraft under § 91.151(b).
- **IFR at any point.** If the flight is conducted IFR, § 91.167 governs (45 minutes plus alternate fuel). If the flight *begins* VFR and later picks up an IFR clearance, § 91.151(b) is the test at brake release and § 91.167 governs from the point the IFR clearance is accepted — prudent planning satisfies the higher of the two for the portion flown IFR.
- **Part 121/135 or exemptions.** Those operators are subject to their own fuel rules and OpSpecs; § 91.151(b) is the Part 91 baseline. The 20-minute figure is unchanged in the Part 135 VFR-helicopter case, but OpSpecs can be more restrictive.
- **Jurisdiction.** This is federal (FAA) law. State law does not set fuel reserves; military operations are governed separately (e.g., service regulations) and are outside this answer.

## 7. Assumptions carried

1. Civilian US flight conducted under 14 CFR Part 91.
2. Entirely VFR — no portion flown under IFR.
3. "Reserve" means the regulatory minimum, not a company or personal minimum.
4. Fuel quantities are usable fuel.
5. "Normal cruising speed" is the speed used for the flight's cruise segment; the reserve burn rate is taken at that condition.

## 8. One-line answer for the flight plan

> Reserve: **20 minutes** at normal cruising speed beyond the first point of intended landing (14 CFR 91.151(b)); no day/night adjustment for rotorcraft.

Abstract
This document formally deprecates Transport Layer
Security (TLS) versions 1.0 (RFC 2246) and 1.1 (RFC 4346).
Accordingly, those documents have been moved
to Historic status. These versions lack support for current
and recommended cryptographic algorithms and mechanisms, and
various government and industry profiles of applications using
TLS now mandate avoiding these old TLS versions. TLS version 1.2
became the recommended version for IETF protocols in 2008
(subsequently being obsoleted by TLS version 1.3 in 2018), providing
sufficient time to transition away from older versions.
Removing support for older versions from implementations reduces the
attack surface, reduces opportunity for misconfiguration, and
streamlines library and product maintenance.¶
This document also deprecates Datagram TLS (DTLS) version 1.0
(RFC 4347) but not DTLS version 1.2, and there is no DTLS
version 1.1.¶
This document updates many RFCs that normatively refer to TLS version 1.0 or
TLS version 1.1, as described herein. This document also updates the best
practices for TLS usage in RFC 7525; hence, it is part of BCP 195.¶
Status of This Memo
This memo documents an Internet Best Current Practice.¶

Transport Layer Security (TLS) versions 1.0 [RFC2246]
and 1.1 [RFC4346] were superseded by TLS 1.2 [RFC5246] in 2008, which has now itself been superseded by
TLS 1.3 [RFC8446]. Datagram Transport Layer Security
(DTLS) version 1.0 [RFC4347] was superseded by DTLS 1.2
[RFC6347] in 2012.  Therefore, it is timely to further
deprecate TLS 1.0, TLS 1.1, and DTLS 1.0.
Accordingly, the aforementioned documents have been moved to Historic status.¶
Technical reasons for deprecating these versions include:¶
They require the implementation of older cipher suites that are no
longer desirable for cryptographic reasons, e.g., TLS 1.0 makes
TLS_DHE_DSS_WITH_3DES_EDE_CBC_SHA mandatory to implement.¶
There is a lack of support for current recommended cipher suites, especially
authenticated encryption with associated data (AEAD) ciphers,
which were not supported prior to TLS 1.2. Note that
registry entries for no-longer-desirable ciphersuites remain in the
registries, but many TLS registries were updated by [RFC8447], which indicates that such entries are not
recommended by the IETF.¶
The integrity of the handshake depends on SHA-1 hash.¶
The authentication of the peers depends on SHA-1 signatures.¶

Acknowledgements
Authors' Addresses
1.  Introduction
Transport Layer Security (TLS) versions 1.0 [RFC2246] and 1.1
[RFC4346] were superseded by TLS 1.2 [RFC5246] in 2008, which has now
itself been superseded by TLS 1.3 [RFC8446].  Datagram Transport
Layer Security (DTLS) version 1.0 [RFC4347] was superseded by DTLS
1.2 [RFC6347] in 2012.  Therefore, it is timely to further deprecate
TLS 1.0, TLS 1.1, and DTLS 1.0.  Accordingly, the aforementioned
documents have been moved to Historic status.
Technical reasons for deprecating these versions include:
*  They require the implementation of older cipher suites that are no
longer desirable for cryptographic reasons, e.g., TLS 1.0 makes
TLS_DHE_DSS_WITH_3DES_EDE_CBC_SHA mandatory to implement.
*  There is a lack of support for current recommended cipher suites,
especially authenticated encryption with associated data (AEAD)
ciphers, which were not supported prior to TLS 1.2.  Note that
registry entries for no-longer-desirable ciphersuites remain in
the registries, but many TLS registries were updated by [RFC8447],
which indicates that such entries are not recommended by the IETF.
*  The integrity of the handshake depends on SHA-1 hash.

verdict.summary:
TECHNICAL NOTE — Deprecation of TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1

1. Answers

(1) The RFC that deprecated TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 is RFC 8996, "Deprecating TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1" (K. Moriarty, S. Farrell; March 2021; Standards-track-adjacent status: Best Current Practice, part of BCP 195; DOI 10.17487/RFC8996; 18 pages; produced from draft-ietf-tls-oldversions-deprecate-12).

(2) The status it gave to the RFCs that defined those versions — RFC 2246 (TLS 1.0) and RFC 4346 (TLS 1.1) — is Historic. Both documents were moved to Historic status.

2. Evidence (verbatim, from the RFC Editor text)

Abstract of RFC 8996:
  "This document formally deprecates Transport Layer Security (TLS) versions 1.0 (RFC 2246) and 1.1 (RFC 4346). Accordingly, those documents have been moved to Historic status."

Section 1 (Introduction) of RFC 8996:
  "Transport Layer Security (TLS) versions 1.0 [RFC2246] and 1.1 [RFC4346] were superseded by TLS 1.2 [RFC5246] in 2008 ... Therefore, it is timely to further deprecate TLS 1.0, TLS 1.1, and DTLS 1.0. Accordingly, the aforementioned documents have been moved to Historic status."

Metadata record (rfc8996.json):
  title: Deprecating TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1; pub_status: BEST CURRENT PRACTICE; status: BEST CURRENT PRACTICE; pub_date: March 2021; obsoletes: RFC5469, RFC7507; updates: ~80 RFCs including RFC3261, RFC3552, RFC5246-adjacent profiles, RFC6347, RFC7525.

Datatracker document history: revision "RFC 8996 (2021-03-23)" — i.e., publication day 23 March 2021, consistent with the month-level 'March 2021' in the JSON metadata.

3. The two distinct acts — do not conflate them

RFC 8996 performs two separate normative actions, and the question's two asks map onto them one-for-one:

  a) Deprecation (the verb in the title): the document formally deprecates the *protocol versions* TLS 1.0, TLS 1.1, and DTLS 1.0. This is a BCP 195 statement of IETF consensus that the versions must not be used.
  b) Status change: the document moves the *defining documents* to Historic. Historic is an RFC status under RFC 2026 (the document is no longer a candidate for implementation; it is retained for archival/historical reference).

So the answer to ask 1 is a document identifier (RFC 8996); the answer to ask 2 is an RFC status word (Historic). "Deprecated" is not an RFC status; "Historic" is. Answering ask 2 with "deprecated" would be wrong.

4. Scope of the status change — what exactly went Historic

Documents moved to Historic by RFC 8996:
  - RFC 2246 — The TLS Protocol Version 1.0  (the document named in ask 2)
  - RFC 4346 — The Transport Layer Security (TLS) Protocol Version 1.1  (the document named in ask 2)
  - RFC 4347 — Datagram Transport Layer Security Version 1.0 (DTLS 1.0; the Abstract explicitly deprecates DTLS 1.0 but NOT DTLS 1.2, and notes there is no DTLS 1.1)
  - RFC 5469 — DES and IDEA Cipher Suites for TLS (moved to Historic because the only TLS versions for which their use is defined are now Historic; RFC 5469 is also listed in the metadata under 'obsoletes')

Documents obsoleted (not merely made Historic):
  - RFC 5469 (see above)
  - RFC 7507 — TLS Fallback SCSV, whose function is superseded by the TLS 1.3 ServerHello.Random sentinel mechanism

Note on metadata: RFC 8996's 'obsoletes' list contains only RFC5469 and RFC7507 — RFC 2246 and RFC 4346 are *not* in that list, because they were already superseded (by RFC 5246 in 2008, itself superseded by RFC 8446 in 2018). The Historic move is effected by the document's normative prose and reflected in the RFC Editor's status metadata for RFC 2246 and RFC 4346 themselves, not by an 'obsoletes' relation in RFC 8996's header. Anyone verifying by grepping only the 'obsoletes' field will miss the answer to ask 2; verify against the Abstract/Introduction text and against the individual metadata pages for RFC 2246 and RFC 4346.

5. Rationale recorded in RFC 8996 (for context in a change-control or audit note)

  - TLS 1.0/1.1 mandate old cipher suites (e.g., TLS 1.0 makes TLS_DHE_DSS_WITH_3DES_EDE_CBC_SHA mandatory to implement).
  - No support for AEAD cipher suites (not available before TLS 1.2).
  - Handshake integrity depends on SHA-1; peer authentication depends on SHA-1 signatures.
  - Supporting four TLS protocol versions increases the likelihood of misconfiguration.
  - TLS 1.2 was the IETF-recommended version from 2008 and TLS 1.3 from 2018, so ample migration time had elapsed.

6. Verification procedure (for an engineer re-checking this)

  a) Fetch https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8996.txt (or .html) and read the Abstract and Section 1; confirm the two sentences quoted in section 2 above.
  b) Fetch https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8996.json and confirm status = BEST CURRENT PRACTICE, pub_date = March 2021, and the obsoletes/updates lists.
  c) Fetch https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc2246 and https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc4346 and confirm each now shows Status: Historic.
  d) Fetch https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc8996/ and confirm the BCP 195 association and the 2021-03-23 publication date.
  Negative check: if any source says 'Obsoletes: RFC 2246' on RFC 8996, it is wrong; RFC 2246 was obsoleted by RFC 5246, not by RFC 8996.

7. One-line answer

RFC 8996, "Deprecating TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1" (March 2021, BCP 195), deprecated TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 and moved their defining RFCs, RFC 2246 and RFC 4346, to Historic status.

Contribution & Benefit Base
Wage-indexed Amounts
Method for determining the base
The formula for determining the OASDI contribution and benefit base
is set by law. The formula is applicable only if a
cost-of-living increase becomes
effective for December of the year in which a determination of
the base would ordinarily be made.  Because there is a cost-of-living increase for December 2026, the
formula is applicable.  The formula states that the base for any year
Y after 1994 is equal to the 1994 base of $60,600 multiplied by
the ratio of the national average wage index for
year (Y-2) to that for 1992, with the result rounded to the nearest
multiple of $300.  If the result is less than the current base, the base
is not reduced.
Base for 2027
Under the above formula, the base for 2027 shall be the 1994 base of $60,600
multiplied by the ratio of the national average wage index for 2025 to that for
1992, or, if larger, the 2026 base of $184,500.  If the amount so determined
is not a multiple of $300, it is rounded to the nearest multiple of $300.

verdict.summary:
ANSWER

The US Social Security contribution and benefit base (the OASDI taxable maximum, i.e. the maximum amount of earnings subject to the Social Security payroll tax) for calendar year 2026 is $184,500.

- Year: 2026 (wages paid/earned in the 2026 calendar year)
- Amount: $184,500.00
- Unit: US dollars
- Status: officially determined and published, not a projection
- Immediately prior year, for comparison: $176,100 (2025); following year already announced: $192,300 (2027)

WHAT THE FIGURE MEANS OPERATIONALLY

1. Employee and employer. The OASDI rate for 2026 is 6.2% each for employee and employer. Maximum employee withholding for 2026 = $184,500 x 6.2% = $11,439.00; the employer owes the identical $11,439.00. Combined OASDI on a maxed-out worker = $22,878.00.
2. Self-employed. The OASDI rate on self-employment income is 12.4% up to the same $184,500 base. Maximum 2026 OASDI self-employment tax = $184,500 x 12.4% = $22,878.00 (before the income-tax deduction for one-half of SE tax). The base is identical for employees and the self-employed; only the rate differs.
3. Medicare is NOT capped. The Hospital Insurance (HI) portion is 1.45% each on all wages with no wage base limit, plus the 0.9% Additional Medicare Tax above $200,000 single / $250,000 married-filing-jointly. The $184,500 figure applies to OASDI only and must not be applied to the Medicare portion.
4. Benefit computation. The same annual limit applies when those earnings are used in a benefit computation (wage-indexed earnings credited for OASDI benefit purposes are capped at the same base).
5. Form W-2 / payroll administration. Social Security wages (W-2 box 3) and Social Security tax withheld (box 4) are capped using $184,500 for 2026; Medicare wages (box 5) are not capped. Reporting guidance for 2026 explicitly instructs employers to ensure no employee's Social Security wage amount exceeds $184,500.
6. Related 2026 figures for context (not the answer to the ask): 'old-law' contribution and benefit base for 2026 = $137,100; quarter of coverage = $1,890; COLA effective December 2025 = 2.8%.

STATUTORY BASIS AND DERIVATION CHECK (why $184,500 is the correct arithmetic result, not just a quoted number)

The base is set by the automatic-adjustment formula in the Social Security Act: for any year Y after 1994, base(Y) = $60,600 (the 1994 base) x [NAWI(Y-2) / NAWI(1992)], rounded to the nearest multiple of $300, and never reduced below the prior year's base. The formula applies only if a cost-of-living increase is effective for December of the year in which the determination is made.

For 2026: Y-2 = 2024, NAWI(2024) = $69,846.57, NAWI(1992) = $22,935.42.
  $60,600 x ($69,846.57 / $22,935.42) = $60,600 x 3.045358 = $184,548.7
  Rounded to the nearest $300: $184,548.7 / 300 = 615.16 -> 615 x $300 = $184,500
  $184,500 > $176,100 (2025 base), so the no-decrease floor does not bind.
This reproduces the published $184,500 exactly and is the same formula and method SSA shows on its determination page (which now runs the identical computation forward to 2027: $60,600 x 72,800.33 / 22,935.42 = $192,353.14 -> $192,300, with the note that the comparison is made against 'the 2026 base of $184,500').

SOURCES (all official, all agreeing)

1. SSA, '2026 Social Security Changes' COLA fact sheet (ssa.gov/news/en/cola/factsheets/2026.html): Maximum Taxable Earnings, Social Security (OASDI only) - 2025 $176,100; 2026 $184,500; Medicare (HI only) - No Limit.
2. SSA Office of the Chief Actuary, 'Contribution and Benefit Base' table (ssa.gov/oact/cola/cbb.html): 2025 $176,100; 2026 $184,500; 2027 $192,300.
3. SSA Office of the Chief Actuary, 'Contribution and Benefit Base Determination' (ssa.gov/oact/cola/cbbdet.html): formula, inputs, rounding rule, and the statement that the 2027 base is computed against 'the 2026 base of $184,500'.
4. IRS Publication 15 (2026), Employer's Tax Guide (irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/p15.pdf), dated Dec 15, 2025: 'The social security wage base limit is $184,500' (stated in 'What's New' and again in the tax-rate discussion), with 6.2% each for employer and employee and no Medicare wage base limit.
5. SSA Detailed Calculator update page (ssa.gov/oact/anypia/update.html): lists 'Contribution and benefit base for 2026: $184,500' among the announced automatic amounts.

SCOPE, ASSUMPTIONS AND LIMITS OF THIS ANSWER

- The ask is the OASDI wage base for 2026 only. It is answered directly; no projection or estimate is involved, so no estimate caveat is required. The value has been formally determined and appears in IRS's 2026 employer guidance.
- The figure is the wage base for 2026 regardless of when it was announced (announced in fall 2025 with the 2.8% COLA).
- This answer deliberately does not substitute the 2025 ($176,100) or 2027 ($192,300) figures, which appear in the sources only as adjacent-year context.
- The 2026 base is a statutory/automatic-adjustment figure; it is not affected by the 2026 legislative changes referenced in IRS Pub 15 (P.L. 119-21, individual rate extensions), which do not alter the OASDI taxable maximum.
- Nothing in the ask is blocked: the value is officially published and corroborated by four independent official documents.

Social Security's Old-Age, Survivors, and Disability
Insurance (OASDI) program limits the amount of earnings subject to taxation for
a given year.  The same annual limit also applies when those earnings are used
in a benefit computation.  This limit changes each year with changes
in the national average wage index.  We call this annual
limit the contribution and benefit base.  This amount is also commonly referred
to as the taxable maximum. For earnings in 2027, this base is
$192,300.
The OASDI tax rate for wages paid in
2027 is set by statute at 6.2 percent for employees and employers, each.

IR-2025-111, Nov. 13, 2025
WASHINGTON — The Internal Revenue Service announced today that the amount individuals can contribute to their 401(k) plans in 2026 has increased to $24,500, up from $23,500 for 2025.
The IRS today also issued technical guidance regarding all cost‑of‑living adjustments affecting dollar limitations for pension plans and other retirement-related items for tax year 2026 in Notice 2025-67 PDF, posted today on IRS.gov.
Highlights of changes for 2026
The annual contribution limit for employees who participate in 401(k), 403(b), governmental 457 plans, and the federal government’s Thrift Savings Plan is increased to $24,500, up from $23,500 for 2025.
The limit on annual contributions to an IRA is increased to $7,500 from $7,000. The IRA catch‑up contribution limit for individuals aged 50 and over was amended under the SECURE 2.0 Act of 2022 (SECURE 2.0) to include an annual cost‑of‑living adjustment is increased to $1,100, up from $1,000 for 2025.

For single taxpayers covered by a workplace retirement plan, the phase-out range is increased to between $81,000 and $91,000, up from between $79,000 and $89,000 for 2025.
For married couples filing jointly, if the spouse making the IRA contribution is covered by a workplace retirement plan, the phase-out range is increased to between $129,000 and $149,000, up from between $126,000 and $146,000 for 2025.
For an IRA contributor who is not covered by a workplace retirement plan and is married to someone who is covered, the phase-out range is increased to between $242,000 and $252,000, up from between $236,000 and $246,000 for 2025.
For a married individual filing a separate return who is covered by a workplace retirement plan, the phase-out range is not subject to an annual cost-of-living adjustment and remains between $0 and $10,000.
Other phase-out ranges and limitations

The amount individuals can generally contribute to their SIMPLE retirement accounts is increased to $17,000, up from $16,500 for 2025. Pursuant to a change made in SECURE 2.0, individuals can contribute a higher amount to certain applicable SIMPLE retirement accounts. For 2026, this higher amount is increased to $18,100, up from $17,600 for 2025.
The catch-up contribution limit that generally applies for employees aged 50 and over who participate in most SIMPLE plans is increased to $4,000, up from $3,500 for 2025. Under a change made in SECURE 2.0, a different catch-up limit applies for employees aged 50 and over who participate in certain applicable SIMPLE plans, which remains $3,850. Under a change made in SECURE 2.0, a higher catch-up contribution limit applies for employees aged 60, 61, 62 and 63 who participate in SIMPLE plans, which remains $5,250.
Details on these and other retirement-related cost-of-living adjustments for 2026 are in Notice 2025-67, available on IRS.gov.

verdict.summary:
# 2026 401(k) Elective Deferral Limit (IRC §402(g)) — HR/Benefits Answer

## Answer

**$24,500.**

For the 2026 calendar year, an employee's elective deferrals to a 401(k) plan are limited to **$24,500**, before any catch-up contribution. This is the basic elective deferral limit under IRC §402(g)(1), as adjusted for cost-of-living. It is up from $23,500 for 2025.

## Authority

The figure is final and published, not projected. The IRS released the 2026 cost-of-living adjustments on **November 13, 2025**, in **IR-2025-111**, with the technical guidance in **Notice 2025-67**:

- IR-2025-111: "The Internal Revenue Service announced today that the amount individuals can contribute to their 401(k) plans in 2026 has increased to $24,500, up from $23,500 for 2025."
- Notice 2025-67: "The limitation under section 402(g)(1) on the exclusion for elective deferrals described in section 402(g)(3), which includes elective deferrals made to the Thrift Savings Plan, is increased from $23,500 to $24,500."
- IRS Retirement Topics — 401(k) and Profit-Sharing Plan Contribution Limits: "The limit on employee elective deferrals (for traditional and safe harbor plans) is: $24,500 in 2026, subject to cost-of-living adjustments."
- IRS Publication 560: "The limit on elective deferrals, other than catch-up contributions, is $23,500 for 2025 and $24,500 for 2026."

Because the number is published in a Notice, no further confirmation step is required before programming payroll. It remains subject to statutory cost-of-living adjustment in later years (the 2027 figure is already announced separately and is **not** applicable to 2026 — see "Do not use" below).

## What the $24,500 does and does not cover

**Included under the single $24,500 cap:**
- Pre-tax (traditional) elective deferrals.
- Designated Roth elective deferrals. **Roth and pre-tax deferrals share one combined $24,500 limit** — a participant cannot defer $24,500 pre-tax *and* $24,500 Roth.
- Deferrals to a safe harbor 401(k) (the safe harbor status does not raise the §402(g) limit).
- Elective deferrals the employee makes to **any other** 401(k), 403(b), SARSEP, SIMPLE, or governmental 457(b) plan during 2026. The §402(g) limit is an **individual, aggregate** limit across all such plans, not a per-plan limit. Multiple employers do not multiply it.

**Not counted against the $24,500:**
- Age-50-and-over catch-up contributions ($8,000 for 2026), which are added on top.
- Ages 60–63 enhanced catch-up contributions ($11,250 for 2026), which are added on top.
- Employer match and employer nonelective contributions (these are governed by §415(c), not §402(g)).
- After-tax (non-Roth) employee contributions, if the plan permits them (governed by §415(c)).

**Not the same limit — do not apply $24,500 here:**
- **SIMPLE 401(k) plans:** $17,000 for 2026 (with a $4,000 age-50 catch-up, or $5,250 for ages 60–63).
- **§457(e)(15) governmental/tax-exempt 457(b) deferrals:** also $24,500 for 2026, but that is a separate Code section that happens to land on the same number. A 457(b) deferral does not reduce the 401(k) §402(g) limit for a governmental plan participant in the way SIMPLE/401(k)/403(b) deferrals do, so handle 457(b) coordination per plan counsel.
- **Starter 401(k) deferral-only arrangements (§401(k)(16)):** $6,000 for 2026.

## Companion 2026 figures (for context and for checking payroll logic)

| Item | 2026 | Code section |
|---|---|---|
| Elective deferral limit (the answer) | **$24,500** | §402(g)(1) |
| Catch-up, age 50+ | $8,000 | §414(v)(2)(B)(i) |
| Catch-up, ages 60–63 | $11,250 | §414(v)(2)(E)(i) |
| Maximum deferrals, participant age 50+ | $32,500 (= 24,500 + 8,000) | §402(g) + §414(v) |
| Maximum deferrals, participant age 60–63 | $35,750 (= 24,500 + 11,250) | §402(g) + §414(v) |
| Total annual additions (all sources) | $72,000 | §415(c)(1)(A) |
| Compensation limit for contributions/benefits | $360,000 | §401(a)(17) |
| HCE threshold | $160,000 | §414(q)(1)(B) |
| Key employee officer threshold (top-heavy) | $235,000 | §416(i)(1)(A)(i) |
| Mandatory Roth catch-up wage threshold (prior-year wages) | $150,000 | §414(v)(7)(A) |

Consistency note for reviewers: catch-up contributions are **disregarded** when applying the §415(c) $72,000 annual-additions limit, so the $32,500 and $35,750 totals above are not constrained by, and do not encroach on, the $72,000 figure. The §402(g) limit also applies only up to 100% of the employee's compensation — no employee can defer more than they earn.

## Do not use (common 2026 error)

The 2027 limits — $25,500 base deferral, $8,500 age-50 catch-up, $11,250→$11,750 enhanced catch-up, $75,000 §415(c) — apply to taxable years beginning in 2027 and must not be loaded into a 2026 payroll or plan-year configuration.

## Payroll / plan-administration procedure

1. **Configure the annual cap.** Set the employee deferral cap to $24,500 for plan years/calendar years ending in 2026, and the catch-up cap separately ($8,000, or $11,250 for participants attaining 60, 61, 62, or 63 in 2026) if the plan permits catch-up.
2. **Per-pay-period proration.** Divide the annual cap by the number of remaining pay periods, rounding **up** to the cent so the participant can reach — but never exceed — the cap:
   - 26 pay periods: $24,500 / 26 = **$942.31**
   - 24 pay periods: $24,500 / 24 = **$1,020.84**
   - 52 pay periods: $24,500 / 52 = **$471.16**
   - 12 pay periods: $24,500 / 12 = **$2,041.67**
   Alternatively, allow a whole-percentage election and cap the final period at the remaining headroom.
3. **Hard stop at the cap.** The payroll system must stop deferrals once cumulative YTD elective deferrals (pre-tax + Roth) reach $24,500, then, if the participant is catch-up eligible and has elected it, continue up to the applicable catch-up amount. Do not let a percentage election run past the cap and create an excess deferral.
4. **Mid-year hires and mid-year election changes.** Prorate from the date of eligibility or election; do not annualize to a full $24,500 if the participant had deferrals at a prior employer in 2026 that they disclose.
5. **Aggregation across employers.** Capture prior-employer 2026 deferrals on the participant certification/annual questionnaire; the employee — not the plan — is responsible for the aggregate §402(g) test, but the plan should provide the mechanism to reduce deferrals and should correct excess deferrals per EPCRS.
6. **Excess deferral correction.** Deferrals above $24,500 (excluding valid catch-up) are includible in the employee's gross income for 2026 and must be distributed by **April 15, 2027** to avoid double taxation; earnings are taxable in the year of distribution. Notify affected participants promptly.
7. **Nondiscrimination overlay.** The $24,500 is a statutory ceiling, not an entitlement: the plan document may impose a lower limit, and ADP/ACP testing or a safe harbor design may further restrict highly compensated employees' actual deferrals. HCEs may need deferral refunds or recharacterization regardless of the §402(g) headroom.
8. **Roth catch-up readiness.** For 2026, participants whose prior-year FICA wages from the plan sponsor exceeded **$150,000** must make catch-up contributions on a Roth basis if the plan offers Roth. This does not change the $24,500 base limit but does change payroll coding for catch-up dollars.

## Employee-facing one-liner

"For 2026, you can defer up to $24,500 of your pay into the 401(k) on a pre-tax and/or Roth basis combined. If you are 50 or older, you may be able to add up to $8,000 more ($11,250 if you turn 60, 61, 62, or 63 in 2026), subject to your plan's terms."

§ 50.18 National primary ambient air quality standards for PM2.5.




(a) The national primary ambient air quality standards for PM2.5 are 12.0 micrograms per cubic meter (µg/m3) annual arithmetic mean concentration and 35 µg/m3 24-hour average concentration measured in the ambient air as PM2.5 (particles with an aerodynamic diameter less than or equal to a nominal 2.5 micrometers) by either:

(2) An equivalent method designated in accordance with part 53 of this chapt
quotes.whole:
§ 50.18 National primary ambient air quality standards for PM2.5.




(a) The national primary ambient air quality standards for PM2.5 are 12.0 micrograms per cubic meter (µg/m3) annual arithmetic mean concentration and 35 µg/m3 24-hour average concentration measured in the ambient air as PM2.5 (particles with an aerodynamic diameter less than or equal to a nominal 2.5 micrometers) by either:




(1) A reference method based on appendix L to this part and designated in accordance with part 53 of this chapter; or






(2) An equivalent method designated in accordance with part 53 of this chapter.








(b) The primary annual PM2.5 standard is met when the annual arithmetic mean concentration, as determined in accordance with appendix N of this part, is less than or equal to 12.0 µg/m3.





(c) The primary 24-hour PM2.5 standard is met when the 98th percentile 24-hour concentration, as determined in accordance with appendix N of this part, is less than or equal to 35 µg/m3.



[78 FR 3277, Jan. 15, 2013]

Fact Sheet - Reconsideration of National Ambient Air Quality Standards for Particulate Matter (pdf)
(132.6 KB)
On February 7, 2024, EPA strengthened the National Ambient Air Quality Standards for Particulate Matter (PM NAAQS) to protect millions of Americans from harmful and costly health impacts, such as heart attacks and premature death. ​Particle or soot pollution is one of the most dangerous forms of air pollution, and an extensive body of science links it to a range of serious and sometimes deadly illnesses. ​ EPA is setting the level of the primary (health-based) annual PM2.5 standard at 9.0 micrograms per cubic meter to provide increased public health protection, consistent with the available health science.
EPA is not changing the current:
primary and secondary (welfare-based) 24-hour PM2.5 standards,
secondary annual PM2.5 standard, and
primary and secondary PM10 standards.

verdict.summary:
CURRENT US NATIONAL PRIMARY AMBIENT AIR QUALITY STANDARDS FOR PM2.5

ANSWER
- Annual primary standard: 9.0 µg/m³ (annual arithmetic mean concentration)
- 24-hour primary standard: 35 µg/m³ (24-hour average concentration)

AUTHORITATIVE CITATION
40 CFR §50.20, 'National primary ambient air quality standards for PM2.5,' promulgated at 89 FR 16380 (Mar. 6, 2024) — the 2024 reconsideration of the PM NAAQS. Statutory basis: Clean Air Act §109 (42 U.S.C. 7409). Codified text (eCFR, current as of the source fetch on 2026-11-16):
  §50.20(a): 'The national primary ambient air quality standards for PM2.5 are 9.0 micrograms per cubic meter (µg/m3) annual arithmetic mean concentration and 35 µg/m3 24-hour average concentration...'

STATISTICAL FORM (how each level is actually applied — from §50.20(b),(c) and 40 CFR Part 50, Appendix N)
- Annual (9.0 µg/m³): met when the annual arithmetic mean concentration, determined in accordance with Appendix N, is less than or equal to 9.0 µg/m³. Appendix N §4.1: a valid annual PM2.5 design value requires three years of valid annual means (quarterly data capture ≥75% in all four quarters, with an alternative allowance for years having ≥11 creditable samples per quarter under stated conditions); the design value is the 3-year average of annual means, rounded per Appendix N §4.3.
- 24-hour (35 µg/m³): met when the 98th percentile 24-hour concentration, determined in accordance with Appendix N, is less than or equal to 35 µg/m³. Appendix N §4.2: three years of valid annual 98th-percentile values are averaged to produce the 24-hour design value.
- Measurement basis for both: PM2.5 (particles with aerodynamic diameter ≤ nominal 2.5 µm) measured by an FRM based on Appendix L designated under 40 CFR Part 53, or an equivalent method (FEM) designated under Part 53, using only data deemed suitable under Part 58.

WHY 9.0 AND NOT 12.0 — EXPLICIT DISAMBIGUATION
The CFR currently prints more than one PM2.5 section. Do not confuse them:
  §50.20 — 9.0 µg/m³ annual / 35 µg/m³ 24-hour, primary only, 89 FR 16380 (Mar. 6, 2024). THIS IS THE CURRENT OPERATIVE PRIMARY STANDARD.
  §50.18 — 12.0 µg/m³ annual / 35 µg/m³ 24-hour, primary only, 78 FR 3277 (Jan. 15, 2013). Superseded 2012-review primary standard; retained in the codified text (and referenced in Appendix N alongside §50.20 because design values are still computed against both for implementation/classification purposes). Reporting 12.0 µg/m³ as 'current' is the single most common error on this question.
  §50.13 — 15.0 µg/m³ annual / 35 µg/m³ 24-hour, primary and secondary. Older codified text; not the current primary level.
  §50.7 — 15.0 µg/m³ annual / 65 µg/m³ 24-hour, primary and secondary, 62 FR 38711 (July 18, 1997), as amended 69 FR 45595 (July 30, 2004). Original 1997 PM2.5 standards; superseded.

PRIMARY vs SECONDARY (scope note — the request asks for primary only)
§50.20 sets primary (health-based) standards only. EPA's 2024 rule states it did not change the primary and secondary 24-hour PM2.5 standards, the secondary annual PM2.5 standard, or the primary and secondary PM10 standards. The secondary (welfare-based) annual PM2.5 level therefore remains 15.0 µg/m³, and the secondary 24-hour level remains 35 µg/m³ (§50.13). These are NOT the answer to this request; they are given only so the primary figures are not misread.

CURRENCY, AND THE ONE THING TO RE-CHECK BEFORE RELIANCE
EPA's PM NAAQS page (epa.gov/pm-pollution/national-ambient-air-quality-standards-naaqs-pm) carries a dated alert: '03/12/2025 - Trump EPA Announces Path Forward on National Air Quality Standards for Particulate Matter (PM2.5) to Aid Manufacturing, Small Businesses,' with an accompanying reconsideration fact sheet. That is an announced reconsideration, not a codified change: the eCFR text of §50.20 as of the 2026-11-16 source fetch still reads 9.0 µg/m³ annual and 35 µg/m³ 24-hour. The answer above therefore reflects the standards in legal effect, with the caveat that a rulemaking to revise the annual level is in progress and could supersede the 9.0 figure.

RE-VERIFICATION PROCEDURE (run before using these numbers in any permit, SIP, conformity determination, or enforcement/litigation context)
1. Open https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-40/part-50/section-50.20 and read §50.20(a). Confirm the annual figure is still 9.0 µg/m³ and the 24-hour figure still 35 µg/m³.
2. Check §50.18 at https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-40/section-50.18 to confirm it still reads 12.0/35 — if §50.18 has been removed or its figures changed, the codification has moved and step 1 must be re-read.
3. Search the Federal Register (federalregister.gov) for PM NAAQS final rules published after 2024-03-06; any final action revising §50.20 supersedes the annual figure.
4. Check the EPA PM NAAQS page alert banner for the current status of the reconsideration.
5. Confirm the source you are relying on is the primary standard (§50.20), not §50.13 or §50.7.
The 24-hour level of 35 µg/m³ has been unchanged since the 2012 review (78 FR 3277) and is the more stable of the two figures; the annual level is the one that has moved (15.0 → 12.0 in 2012 → 9.0 in 2024) and is the one a reconsideration would most likely change.

UNITS
Micrograms per cubic meter (µg/m³) for both levels, as specified in the codified text. No conversion is required.

BOTTOM LINE
Annual primary PM2.5 NAAQS: 9.0 µg/m³. 24-hour primary PM2.5 NAAQS: 35 µg/m³. Source of record: 40 CFR §50.20 (89 FR 16380, Mar. 6, 2024).

quotes.whole:
Fall hazard means any condition on a walking-working surface that exposes an employee to a risk of harm from a fall on the same level or to a lower level.
Fall protection means any equipment, device, or system that prevents an employee from falling from an elevation or mitigates the effect of such a fall.
Fixed ladder means a ladder with rails or individual rungs that is permanently attached to a structure, building, or equipment. Fixed ladders include individual-rung ladders, but not ship stairs, step bolts, or manhole steps.
Grab bar means an individual horizontal or vertical handhold installed to provide access above the height of the ladder.
Guardrail system means a barrier erected along an unprotected or exposed side, edge, or other area of a walking-working surface to prevent employees from falling to a lower level.
Handrail means a rail used to provide employees with a handhold for support.
Hoist area means any elevated access opening to a walking-working surface through which equipment or materials are loaded or received.
