verdict.summary:
ANSWER

In general industry (US federal OSHA, 29 CFR Part 1910), an employer must protect an employee on a walking-working surface with an unprotected side or edge from falling when that surface is 4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level.

GOVERNING PROVISION

29 CFR 1910.28(b)(1)(i) — Unprotected sides and edges, General:
"Except as provided elsewhere in this section or by other subparts of this part, the employer must ensure that each employee on a walking-working surface with an unprotected side or edge that is 4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level is protected from falling by one or more of the following: (A) Guardrail systems; (B) Safety net systems; or (C) Personal fall protection systems, such as personal fall arrest, travel restraint, or positioning systems."

The identical 4-foot (1.2 m) trigger is restated in the catch-all 29 CFR 1910.28(b)(15) ("Walking-working surfaces not otherwise addressed"), so the figure is not an artifact of one paragraph. It is stable across the 2022, 2023, 2024 and 2025 editions of the CFR and the current eCFR — the Subpart D walking-working surfaces rule (final rule 81 FR 82494, effective January 17, 2017) has not changed the 4-foot trigger.

CITATION FOR VERIFICATION

Primary: 29 CFR 1910.28(b)(1)(i); corroborating: 1910.28(b)(15). Related definitional section: 1910.21(b) (definitions of "unprotected sides and edges," "walking-working surface," "lower level"). System criteria: 1910.29. Training: 1910.30.

SCOPE AND MEASUREMENT

- Scope: general industry walking-working surfaces under Part 1910 Subpart D. Construction work is governed instead by 29 CFR Part 1926 Subpart M, which uses a 6-foot (1.8 m) trigger (1926.501(b)(1)) — this 6-foot figure is a different standard and must not be substituted for the general-industry answer.
- What is measured: the vertical distance from the walking-working surface on which the employee stands to the lower level. The rule is written in terms of the surface being "4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level," not the employee's body part or center of gravity.
- "Unprotected": per 1910.21(b), an unprotected side or edge is any side or edge of a walking-working surface (except at entrances and other points of access) where there is no wall, guardrail system, or stair rail system to protect the employee from falling to a lower level. If a compliant guardrail or wall already exists, the edge is not unprotected and the trigger is not reached.
- At exactly 4 feet the duty attaches ("4 feet or more"); below 4 feet the general edge rule does not require fall protection (though other hazards, e.g., dangerous equipment, may still trigger protection — see below).

RELATED 4-FOOT TRIGGERS IN THE SAME RULE (all consistent with the 4-foot answer)

- Holes (1910.28(b)(3)): holes 4 feet or more above a lower level must be protected by covers, guardrail systems, travel restraint, or personal fall arrest; holes less than 4 feet above a lower level require protection against tripping/stepping into them (covers or guardrails).
- Dangerous equipment (1910.28(b)(6)): an employee less than 4 feet above dangerous equipment must still be protected by a guardrail system or travel restraint system unless the equipment is covered or guarded to eliminate the hazard; at 4 feet or more, guardrail, safety net, travel restraint, or personal fall arrest.
- Openings (1910.28(b)(7)): where the inside bottom edge of the opening is less than 39 inches (99 cm) above the walking-working surface and the outside bottom edge is 4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level, protection is required.
- Stairway landings (1910.28(b)(11)(i)): unprotected side or edge 4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level requires a guardrail or stair rail system.
- Rope descent systems (1910.28(b)(12)(ii)): personal fall arrest system at 4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level.
- Slaughtering facility platforms (1910.28(b)(14)(i)): 4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level.
- Walking-working surfaces not otherwise addressed (1910.28(b)(15)): 4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level.

EXCEPTIONS / CARVE-OUTS THAT DO NOT CHANGE THE GENERAL ANSWER

- Low-slope roofs (1910.28(b)(13)): a distance-based scheme (protection required when work is performed less than 6 feet from the roof edge; designated area / warning line / work rule between 6 and 15 feet; work rule beyond 15 feet, with the infrequent-and-temporary exception). This is a separate paragraph addressing proximity to the edge, not a replacement for the 4-foot general trigger, and it does not raise the general-industry answer.
- Fixed ladders (1910.28(b)(9)): additional requirements attach at 24 feet (7.3 m) above a lower level (personal fall arrest, ladder safety system, or cage/well per the phase-in), but a fixed ladder is also a walking-working surface and the underlying fall-protection duty is not eliminated below 24 feet.
- Scaffolds (1910.28(b)(12)(i)): employees on scaffolds are protected in accordance with 29 CFR Part 1926 Subpart L, not the 4-foot Subpart D trigger.
- Portable ladders are addressed by 1910.23 (use, inspection, three-point contact, etc.) rather than by a fall-protection trigger height in 1910.28.
- Pits less than 10 feet deep (1910.28(b)(8)) have an alternative compliance path (limited access, floor markings or warning line at least 6 feet from the edge, caution signs) rather than conventional guardrail/fall-arrest systems.
- Infeasibility: where the employer can demonstrate that guardrail, safety net, or personal fall protection systems are infeasible or would create a greater hazard, 1910.28(b)(1)(ii) permits a fall protection plan meeting 1910.29(k) — the 4-foot trigger still applies; only the means change.

JURISDICTIONAL NOTE

About half the states and territories operate OSHA-approved State Plans. State Plans must be at least as effective as federal OSHA; some adopt the federal 4-foot figure verbatim, and a few impose stricter requirements for specific operations. The 4-foot figure is the correct federal general-industry answer; a covered employer in a State Plan state should confirm the state's codified text (e.g., Oregon OSHA Division 2, Subdivision D, which mirrors the 4-foot trigger and the definitions quoted above).

PRACTICAL BOTTOM LINE

4 feet (1.2 m). At or above that vertical distance from the walking-working surface to the lower level, an unprotected side or edge must be protected by a guardrail system, safety net system, or personal fall protection system (personal fall arrest, travel restraint, or positioning), with a 1910.29(k) fall protection plan available only where those systems are infeasible or create a greater hazard. Below 4 feet the general edge rule does not apply, but the dangerous-equipment, hole, and pit provisions may still impose duties.

§ 91.151 Fuel requirements for flight in VFR conditions.




(a) No person may begin a flight in an airplane under VFR conditions unless (considering wind and forecast weather conditions) there is enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and, assuming normal cruising speed—




(1) During the day, to fly after that for at least 30 minutes; or






(2) At night, to fly after that for at least 45 minutes.

verdict.summary:
# VFR Helicopter Fuel Reserve — US FAA

## Answer

**20 minutes** of flight time at normal cruising speed, after reaching the first point of intended landing.

Governing rule: **14 CFR § 91.151(b)** — *"No person may begin a flight in a rotorcraft under VFR conditions unless (considering wind and forecast weather conditions) there is enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and, assuming normal cruising speed, to fly after that for at least 20 minutes."*

This is a **time** requirement, not a quantity. It is expressed at normal cruising speed and does **not** vary between day and night for rotorcraft (contrast § 91.151(a) for airplanes: 30 minutes day, 45 minutes night).

## Regulatory basis and scope

| Regime | VFR helicopter reserve after first point of intended landing | Cite |
|---|---|---|
| Part 91 general operating rules (default) | **20 min**, day or night | § 91.151(b) |
| Part 135 air taxi/commuter, VFR helicopter | **20 min**, day or night | § 135.209(b) |
| *(Contrast — not applicable)* Part 91 airplane VFR | 30 min day / 45 min night | § 91.151(a) |
| *(Contrast — not applicable)* IFR helicopter, Part 91 | 30 min after the alternate (when alternate required) | § 91.167(a)(3) |
| *(Contrast — not applicable)* IFR helicopter, Part 135 | 30 min after the alternate (when alternate required) | § 135.223(a)(3) |

The answer is the same 20 minutes under either Part 91 or Part 135 for a VFR helicopter, so the Part 91 vs. Part 135 ambiguity does not change the number. Only IFR flight changes it (30 min), and IFR is outside the question as asked.

Additional points that bound the answer:

1. **No alternate fuel is required for VFR.** The 20 minutes is the entire post-destination increment; there is no VFR equivalent of the IFR alternate-fuel requirement.
2. **The 20 minutes is a floor, not a flight-planning target.** Operations Specifications, company fuel policy, or pilot judgment under § 91.103 (preflight action — become familiar with all available information, including fuel required) may and routinely do require more. The regulation sets the minimum below which flight may not begin.
3. **Day/night and terrain do not change the rotorcraft VFR figure.** Unlike airplanes, there is no night penalty in § 91.151(b) or § 135.209(b).
4. **Currency of text:** the quoted § 91.151(b) is the currently codified eCFR text and contains no day/night rotorcraft split. Any post-2022 Part 91 Subpart B helicopter rulemaking does not, in the codified text relied on here, alter the 20-minute VFR rotorcraft reserve. If an operator's OpSpecs or a future amendment impose a different figure, the more restrictive requirement governs the flight.
5. **Consideration of wind and forecast weather** is mandatory in determining both the en-route fuel and the reserve — the 20 minutes is not to be computed in still air if a headwind is forecast.

## Converting 20 minutes to a fuel quantity

The regulation is satisfied by *time*. To translate it into gallons or pounds for a specific helicopter:

**Reserve fuel = (20 / 60) × normal-cruising-speed fuel consumption = 0.3333 × hourly burn**

Procedure:
1. Take the fuel burn at **normal cruising speed** (not hover, not max-range, not max-endurance power) from the RFM/POH cruise performance table for the planned cruise altitude and temperature.
2. Multiply the hourly burn by 0.3333 (i.e., divide by 3).
3. Add the **unusable fuel** quantity from the RFM (the fuel that cannot be delivered to the engine) — the 20-minute figure must be *usable* fuel.
4. Add the result to the trip fuel computed to the first point of intended landing, then compare against usable fuel on board at brake/takeoff release.
5. Do not credit the reserve with any wind or tailwind assumption, and do not reduce it for climb/descent; the rule specifies normal cruising speed.

**Worked examples (illustrative only — substitute the actual aircraft's POH numbers):**

- Cruise burn 250 lb/hr → reserve = 250 × 0.3333 = **83.3 lb** of usable fuel.
- Cruise burn 30 gal/hr → reserve = 30 × 0.3333 = **10.0 gal** of usable fuel.
- Equivalent still-air distance at 120 kt normal cruise → 120 × 0.3333 = **40 nm** past the first point of intended landing.

## Minimum flight-planning equation (Part 91 VFR helicopter)

```
Required usable fuel at start = Trip fuel to first point of intended landing
                             + Reserve (20 min at normal cruise burn)
                             (+ any operator/OpSpec/company increment, if more restrictive)

Must satisfy:  Usable fuel on board >= Required usable fuel
```

If the check fails, the flight may not begin under § 91.151(b).

## One-line answer for the flight-planning record

> Reserve fuel required: **20 minutes at normal cruising speed beyond the first point of intended landing** (14 CFR 91.151(b); identical under 14 CFR 135.209(b) for Part 135 helicopter VFR operations), computed as usable fuel and adjusted for forecast wind.

RFC 8996
Deprecating TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1
Abstract
This document formally deprecates Transport Layer
Security (TLS) versions 1.0 (RFC 2246) and 1.1 (RFC 4346).
Accordingly, those documents have been moved
to Historic status. These versions lack support for current
and recommended cryptographic algorithms and mechanisms, and
various government and industry profiles of applications using
TLS now mandate avoiding these old TLS versions. TLS version 1.2
became the recommended version for IETF protocols in 2008
(subsequently being obsoleted by TLS version 1.3 in 2018), providing
sufficient time to transition away from older versions.
Removing support for older versions from implementations reduces the
attack surface, reduces opportunity for misconfiguration, and
streamlines library and product maintenance.¶
This document also deprecates Datagram TLS (DTLS) version 1.0
(RFC 4347) but not DTLS version 1.2, and there is no DTLS
version 1.1.¶
This document updates many RFCs that normatively refer to TLS version 1.0 or
TLS version 1.1, as described herein. This document also updates the best
practices for TLS usage in RFC 7525; hence, it is part of BCP 195.¶
Status of This Memo

Transport Layer Security (TLS) versions 1.0 [RFC2246]
and 1.1 [RFC4346] were superseded by TLS 1.2 [RFC5246] in 2008, which has now itself been superseded by
TLS 1.3 [RFC8446]. Datagram Transport Layer Security
(DTLS) version 1.0 [RFC4347] was superseded by DTLS 1.2
[RFC6347] in 2012.  Therefore, it is timely to further
deprecate TLS 1.0, TLS 1.1, and DTLS 1.0.
Accordingly, the aforementioned documents have been moved to Historic status.¶
Technical reasons for deprecating these versions include:¶
They require the implementation of older cipher suites that are no
longer desirable for cryptographic reasons, e.g., TLS 1.0 makes
TLS_DHE_DSS_WITH_3DES_EDE_CBC_SHA mandatory to implement.¶
There is a lack of support for current recommended cipher suites, especially
authenticated encryption with associated data (AEAD) ciphers,
which were not supported prior to TLS 1.2. Note that
registry entries for no-longer-desirable ciphersuites remain in the
registries, but many TLS registries were updated by [RFC8447], which indicates that such entries are not
recommended by the IETF.¶
The integrity of the handshake depends on SHA-1 hash.¶
The authentication of the peers depends on SHA-1 signatures.¶

RFC 9852:   BCP 195: New Protocols Using TLS Must Require TLS 1.3
Best Current Practice
R. Salz
N. Aviram
July 2026
IETF publication
Security Area
Show abstract
Abstract
TLS 1.3 is widely used, has had comprehensive security proofs, and improves both security and privacy deficiencies in TLS 1.2. Therefore, new protocols that use TLS must require TLS 1.3. As DTLS 1.3 is not widely available or deployed, this prescription does not pertain to DTLS (in any DTLS version); it pertains to TLS only.
This document updates RFC 9325. It discusses post-quantum cryptography and the security and privacy improvements in TLS 1.3 as the rationale for the update.

Best Current Practice
K. Moriarty
S. Farrell
March 2021
IETF publication
Security Area
Show abstract
Abstract
This document formally deprecates Transport Layer Security (TLS) versions 1.0 (RFC 2246) and 1.1 (RFC 4346). Accordingly, those documents have been moved to Historic status. These versions lack support for current and recommended cryptographic algorithms and mechanisms, and various government and industry profiles of applications using TLS now mandate avoiding these old TLS versions. TLS version 1.2 became the recommended version for IETF protocols in 2008 (subsequently being obsoleted by TLS version 1.3 in 2018), providing sufficient time to transition away from older versions. Removing support for older versions from implementations reduces the attack surface, reduces opportunity for misconfiguration, and streamlines library and product maintenance.
This document also deprecates Datagram TLS (DTLS) version 1.0 (RFC 4347) but not DTLS version 1.2, and there is no DTLS version 1.1.

quotes.whole:
ISSN: 2070-1721
Deprecating TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1
Abstract
This document formally deprecates Transport Layer Security (TLS)
versions 1.0 (RFC 2246) and 1.1 (RFC 4346).  Accordingly, those
documents have been moved to Historic status.  These versions lack
support for current and recommended cryptographic algorithms and
mechanisms, and various government and industry profiles of
applications using TLS now mandate avoiding these old TLS versions.
TLS version 1.2 became the recommended version for IETF protocols in
2008 (subsequently being obsoleted by TLS version 1.3 in 2018),
providing sufficient time to transition away from older versions.
Removing support for older versions from implementations reduces the
attack surface, reduces opportunity for misconfiguration, and
streamlines library and product maintenance.
This document also deprecates Datagram TLS (DTLS) version 1.0 (RFC
4347) but not DTLS version 1.2, and there is no DTLS version 1.1.
This document updates many RFCs that normatively refer to TLS version
1.0 or TLS version 1.1, as described herein.  This document also
updates the best practices for TLS usage in RFC 7525; hence, it is
part of BCP 195.
Status of This Memo

Acknowledgements
Authors' Addresses
1.  Introduction
Transport Layer Security (TLS) versions 1.0 [RFC2246] and 1.1
[RFC4346] were superseded by TLS 1.2 [RFC5246] in 2008, which has now
itself been superseded by TLS 1.3 [RFC8446].  Datagram Transport
Layer Security (DTLS) version 1.0 [RFC4347] was superseded by DTLS
1.2 [RFC6347] in 2012.  Therefore, it is timely to further deprecate
TLS 1.0, TLS 1.1, and DTLS 1.0.  Accordingly, the aforementioned
documents have been moved to Historic status.
Technical reasons for deprecating these versions include:
*  They require the implementation of older cipher suites that are no
longer desirable for cryptographic reasons, e.g., TLS 1.0 makes
TLS_DHE_DSS_WITH_3DES_EDE_CBC_SHA mandatory to implement.
*  There is a lack of support for current recommended cipher suites,
especially authenticated encryption with associated data (AEAD)
ciphers, which were not supported prior to TLS 1.2.  Note that
registry entries for no-longer-desirable ciphersuites remain in
the registries, but many TLS registries were updated by [RFC8447],
which indicates that such entries are not recommended by the IETF.
*  The integrity of the handshake depends on SHA-1 hash.

verdict.summary:
ANSWER

1) The RFC that deprecated TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 is **RFC 8996**, "Deprecating TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1" (K. Moriarty, S. Farrell; March 2021; part of BCP 195; Internet Best Current Practice). Its abstract opens: "This document formally deprecates Transport Layer Security (TLS) versions 1.0 (RFC 2246) and 1.1 (RFC 4346)."

2) The status it gave the RFCs that had defined those versions is **Historic**. RFC 8996 states, immediately after the deprecation sentence: "Accordingly, those documents have been moved to Historic status." The Introduction repeats it: "Transport Layer Security (TLS) versions 1.0 [RFC2246] and 1.1 [RFC4346] were superseded by TLS 1.2 [RFC5246] in 2008 ... Therefore, it is timely to further deprecate TLS 1.0, TLS 1.1, and DTLS 1.0. Accordingly, the aforementioned documents have been moved to Historic status."

So, specifically:
- RFC 2246 (TLS 1.0, Dierks/Allen, January 1999) — moved to Historic by RFC 8996.
- RFC 4346 (TLS 1.1, Dierks/Rescorla, April 2006) — moved to Historic by RFC 8996.

SUPPORTING DETAIL (from RFC 8996's own text)

- Scope of the deprecation: TLS 1.0 (RFC 2246), TLS 1.1 (RFC 4346), and also DTLS 1.0 (RFC 4347). DTLS 1.2 (RFC 6347) is explicitly *not* deprecated, and "there is no DTLS version 1.1."
- Same reclassification applies to a related document: RFC 5469 (DES/IDEA cipher suites) "has been moved to Historic as well", because the only TLS versions for which those suites are defined are now Historic.
- Documents already Historic (e.g., RFC 6460, RFC 4744, RFC 4743) are merely listed as updated, "in order to reiterate that any usage of the obsolete protocol should use modern TLS."
- Rationale given: TLS 1.0/1.1 lack support for current and recommended cryptographic algorithms and mechanisms (mandatory-to-implement 3DES-based suites, no AEAD ciphers before TLS 1.2, handshake integrity dependent on SHA-1, peer authentication dependent on SHA-1 signatures); government and industry profiles mandate avoiding these versions; TLS 1.2 became the IETF-recommended version in 2008 and was itself obsoleted by TLS 1.3 (RFC 8446) in 2018, giving ample transition time.
- RFC 8996 also updates many RFCs that normatively refer to TLS 1.0/1.1, and updates RFC 7525, which is why it is part of BCP 195.

TERMINOLOGY NOTE (important to state correctly)

In IETF terms, RFC 8996 *deprecates* the protocol versions and *moves the defining documents to Historic status*; it does not itself obsolete RFC 2246 or RFC 4346 with replacement technical content. The technical supersession happened earlier: TLS 1.2 (RFC 5246, 2008) superseded TLS 1.1, and TLS 1.3 (RFC 8446, 2018) superseded TLS 1.2. The correct statement is therefore: RFC 8996 reclassified RFC 2246 and RFC 4346 to Historic, not "obsoleted them".

SOURCES (as fetched, quoted verbatim above)
- https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc8996 — abstract and Section 1 (Introduction).
- https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc8996/ — abstract, "Internet Best Current Practice".
- https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/bcp195/ — RFC 8996 listed as "BCP 195: Deprecating TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1", Best Current Practice, K. Moriarty, S. Farrell, March 2021.
- https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc8996/history/ — RFC 8996 published 2021-03-23 from draft-ietf-tls-oldversions-deprecate.

Social Security's Old-Age, Survivors, and Disability
Insurance (OASDI) program limits the amount of earnings subject to taxation for
a given year.  The same annual limit also applies when those earnings are used
in a benefit computation.  This limit changes each year with changes
in the national average wage index.  We call this annual
limit the contribution and benefit base.  This amount is also commonly referred
to as the taxable maximum. For earnings in 2027, this base is
$192,300.
The OASDI tax rate for wages paid in
2027 is set by statute at 6.2 percent for employees and employers, each. Thus,
an individual with wages equal to or larger than $192,300 would contribute $11,922.60
to the OASDI program in 2027, and his or her employer would contribute the same
amount. The OASDI tax rate for self-employment income in 2027 is 12.4 percent.

Contribution and Benefit Base Determination
Automatic Determinations
Contribution & Benefit Base
Wage-indexed Amounts
Method for determining the base
The formula for determining the OASDI contribution and benefit base
is set by law. The formula is applicable only if a
cost-of-living increase becomes
effective for December of the year in which a determination of
the base would ordinarily be made.  Because there is a cost-of-living increase for December 2026, the
formula is applicable.  The formula states that the base for any year
Y after 1994 is equal to the 1994 base of $60,600 multiplied by
the ratio of the national average wage index for
year (Y-2) to that for 1992, with the result rounded to the nearest
multiple of $300.  If the result is less than the current base, the base
is not reduced.
Base for 2027
Under the above formula, the base for 2027 shall be the 1994 base of $60,600
multiplied by the ratio of the national average wage index for 2025 to that for
1992, or, if larger, the 2026 base of $184,500.  If the amount so determined
is not a multiple of $300, it is rounded to the nearest multiple of $300.

verdict.summary:
ANSWER

The US Social Security contribution and benefit base (the OASDI taxable maximum — the maximum amount of an individual's annual earnings subject to the Social Security payroll tax) for tax year 2026 is $184,500.

This is an officially published figure, not a projection. It was announced by the Social Security Administration in the 2026 COLA/benefit-change fact sheet and is carried in SSA's contribution-and-benefit-base table and in SSA Publication 42-007 (EFW2 specifications) for tax year 2026.

1. PRIMARY SOURCES (all SSA, all agreeing)

  a) SSA, "2026 Social Security Changes" fact sheet (https://www.ssa.gov/cola/factsheets/2026.html), table "Maximum Taxable Earnings":
       Social Security (OASDI only): 2025 = $176,100 ; 2026 = $184,500
       Medicare (HI only): No Limit
     Same page: employee/self-employed combined FICA rate 7.65% / 15.30% in both 2025 and 2026, with the note that the Social Security (OASDI) portion is 6.2% on earnings up to the taxable maximum and the Medicare (HI) portion is 1.45% on all earnings.

  b) SSA Office of the Chief Actuary, "Contribution and Benefit Base" (https://www.ssa.gov/oact/cola/cbb.html), year table:
       2024 = $168,600 ; 2025 = $176,100 ; 2026 = $184,500 ; 2027 = $192,300
     Same page: the annual limit applies both to earnings subject to OASDI taxation and to earnings used in a benefit computation; it changes each year with the national average wage index.

  c) SSA Publication No. 42-007, EFW2 Tax Year 2026 (https://www.ssa.gov/employer/efw/26efw2.pdf):
       Appendix H — Maximum Wage and Tax Table: 2026, employer/employee rate 6.200%, maximum amount of taxed earnings $184,500.00, employee maximum annual tax $11,439.00, minimum household covered wages $3,000.00; Medicare 1.450% with no maximum.
       Body text: Social Security wages plus Social Security tips "should not exceed the annual maximum Social Security wage base for the tax year ($184,500 for tax year 2026)"; Social Security tax withheld "should not exceed $11,439.00 for tax year 2026."

2. HOW THE FIGURE IS PRODUCED (statutory mechanism, for auditability)

The base is not set by annual legislation; it is determined by the automatic-adjustment formula in the Social Security Act. Per SSA's determination page (https://www.ssa.gov/oact/cola/cbbdet.html), the base for any year Y after 1994 equals the 1994 base of $60,600 multiplied by the ratio of the national average wage index (NAWI) for year Y-2 to the NAWI for 1992, rounded to the nearest multiple of $300, and never reduced below the prior year's base. The formula applies only if a cost-of-living increase is effective for December of the year the determination is made. The 2026 base was set by that formula using the 2024 NAWI; the same page's 2027 determination explicitly uses "the 2026 base of $184,500" as its floor comparison, confirming the 2026 value.

Rounding check: $184,500 / $300 = 615 exactly, so the published figure is a valid multiple of $300 as the statute requires. The neighboring years satisfy the same test ($176,100 / 300 = 587; $192,300 / 300 = 641), and the sequence is monotone: $176,100 (2025) < $184,500 (2026) < $192,300 (2027).

3. PAYROLL APPLICATION (derived arithmetic, verified against the official maximum-tax figure)

  - Employee OASDI: 6.2% of earnings up to $184,500 => maximum annual employee OASDI contribution = 184,500 x 0.062 = $11,439.00. This matches SSA's published EFW2 figure of $11,439.00 exactly.
  - Employer OASDI: matching 6.2%, same $11,439.00 maximum.
  - Combined employer + employee OASDI at the cap: 2 x $11,439.00 = $22,878.00.
  - Self-employed OASDI: 12.4% of self-employment income up to $184,500 => $22,878.00 (derived: 184,500 x 0.124); this equals the combined employee + employer amount above, as expected.
  - Medicare (HI): 1.45% employee + 1.45% employer on all earnings, no cap; additional 0.9% Medicare tax on earned income above $200,000 single / $250,000 married filing jointly, which is outside the OASDI base and outside the 7.65% combined rate quoted above.
  - Combined employee FICA at or above the cap: $11,439.00 OASDI + 1.45% of all wages (HI, uncapped). The 7.65% combined rate applies in full only up to $184,500; above that only the 1.45% HI portion (plus any additional Medicare tax) continues.
  - The same $184,500 limit caps earnings creditable toward Social Security benefits for 2026, not just taxable earnings.

4. SCOPE — WHAT THIS NUMBER IS AND IS NOT

  - It is the federal OASDI contribution and benefit base for tax year 2026 only. The base is re-indexed every year, so it must always be year-tagged; 2027 is already published at $192,300 and must not be used for 2026 (or vice versa).
  - It is not the Medicare wage base: HI has had no taxable maximum since 1993.
  - It is not the "old-law" contribution and benefit base, a separate statutory figure used by the Railroad Retirement program, the Pension Benefit Guaranty Corporation, and SSA for years-of-coverage/special-minimum-benefit determinations; the old-law base for 2026 is $137,100, materially lower than the current-law $184,500.
  - It is not the retirement earnings test exempt amounts ($24,480/yr or $2,040/mo under full retirement age; $65,160/yr or $5,430/mo in the year full retirement age is reached) and not the quarter-of-coverage amount ($1,890 for 2026). Those are benefit-eligibility parameters, not the tax base.
  - It is a federal figure; no state wage base is implied.

5. VERIFICATION CHECKLIST FOR A DOWNSTREAM USER

  - Confirm the year label on any payroll table says 2026 and the OASDI maximum is $184,500 (2025's $176,100 and 2027's $192,300 are the common stale/early copies).
  - Confirm the OASDI rate is 6.2% employee / 6.2% employer / 12.4% self-employed, and that the 7.65% / 15.30% combined rates are not applied to earnings above $184,500.
  - Confirm the maximum employee OASDI withholding for 2026 is $11,439.00 (EFW2 field 221-231 check) and that Social Security wages + tips per employee do not exceed $184,500.
  - Cross-check any secondary source (news, payroll vendor, tax calculator) against ssa.gov/cola/factsheets/2026.html or ssa.gov/oact/cola/cbb.html; the SSA fact sheet and the EFW2 Appendix H are the controlling payroll references.

Social Security's Old-Age, Survivors, and Disability
Insurance (OASDI) program limits the amount of earnings subject to taxation for
a given year.  The same annual limit also applies when those earnings are used
in a benefit computation.  This limit changes each year with changes
in the national average wage index.  We call this annual
limit the contribution and benefit base.  This amount is also commonly referred
to as the taxable maximum. For earnings in 2027, this base is
$192,300.
The OASDI tax rate for wages paid in
2027 is set by statute at 6.2 percent for employees and employers, each.

Basic elective deferral limit
The basic limit on elective deferrals is $24,500 in 2026, $23,500 in 2025, $23,000 in 2024 and $22,500 in 2023, or 100% of the employee's compensation, whichever is less. The elective deferral limit for SIMPLE plans is 100% of compensation or $17,000 in 2026, $16,500 in 2025, $16,000 in 2024, and $15,500 in 2023. Catch-up contributions may also be allowed if the employee is age 50 or older.
If the employee's total contributions exceed the deferral limit, the difference is included in the employee's gross income.
Time for depositing elective deferrals
Employers must deposit employee contributions to the retirement plan's trust or individual accounts as soon as they can reasonably be segregated from the employer's general assets. The Department of Labor provides a 7-business-day safe harbor rule for employee contributions to plans with fewer than 100 participants.

quotes.whole:
Employer contributions
Employer matching contributions. If the plan document permits, the employer can make matching contributions for an employee who contributes elective deferrals (for example, 50 cents for each dollar deferred). Employer matching contributions can be discretionary (contributed in some years and not in others, depending on the company's decision) or mandatory, as in SIMPLE plans and Safe Harbor 401(k) plans.
Employer discretionary or non-elective contributions. If the plan document permits, the employer can make contributions other than matching contributions for participants. These contributions are made on behalf of all employees who are plan participants, including participants who choose not to contribute elective deferrals.
Types of employee contributions
Salary reduction/elective deferral contributions are pre-tax employee contributions that are a generally a percentage of the employee's compensation. Some plans permit the employee to contribute a specific dollar amount each pay period. 401(k), 403(b) or SIMPLE IRA plans may permit elective deferral contributions.

verdict.summary:
ANSWER

The limit on an employee's elective deferrals to a 401(k) plan for tax year 2026, before any catch-up contribution, is $24,500.

That is the IRC §402(g)(1) limit on the exclusion for elective deferrals for 2026, up from $23,500 for 2025. It is also capped at 100% of the employee's compensation, whichever is less — for any employee with compensation at or above $24,500 the operative figure is simply $24,500.

AUTHORITY

- IRS Notice 2025-67, '2026 Amounts Relating to Retirement Plans and IRAs, as Adjusted for Changes in Cost-of-Living': 'The limitation under section 402(g)(1) on the exclusion for elective deferrals described in section 402(g)(3) ... is increased from $23,500 to $24,500.'
- IRS, Retirement Topics — 401(k) and Profit-Sharing Plan Contribution Limits: 'The limit on employee elective deferrals (for traditional and safe harbor plans) is: $24,500 in 2026, subject to cost-of-living adjustments.'
- IRS, Retirement Topics — Contributions: 'The basic limit on elective deferrals is $24,500 in 2026, $23,500 in 2025 ... or 100% of the employee's compensation, whichever is less.'
- IRS Publication 560: 'The limit on elective deferrals, other than catch-up contributions, is $23,500 for 2025 and $24,500 for 2026.'
- IRS Publication 525 (2026 draft): 'For 2026, you shouldn't have deferred more than a total of $24,500.'

HOW TO APPLY IT (scope boundaries that determine whether $24,500 is the right number for a given employee)

1. This is the §402(g) employee elective deferral limit only. It is not the §415(c) total annual additions limit, which for 2026 is $72,000 and covers employee deferrals plus employer match, nonelective contributions, and forfeiture allocations. $24,500 is a component of, and well below, the $72,000 figure.
2. Catch-up contributions are excluded, as the question specifies. For 2026 the age-50-and-over catch-up limit for a non-SIMPLE 401(k) is $8,000, and the higher SECURE 2.0 catch-up limit for participants who attain age 60, 61, 62, or 63 in 2026 is $11,250. Those amounts sit on top of the $24,500 and are not reduced by it; conversely the $24,500 is not reduced by them.
3. The limit is per individual, not per plan or per employer. An employee aggregates elective deferrals across all 401(k), 403(b), SARSEP, and SIMPLE plans in which they participate when testing against the overall limit, and across all plans of the same employer plus its controlled group and affiliated service group members.
4. Pre-tax and designated Roth elective deferrals share the same $24,500 limit; electing Roth does not create additional room.
5. SIMPLE 401(k) plans are different: the 2026 SIMPLE deferral limit is $17,000 (with its own catch-up of $4,000, or $5,250 for ages 60–63). If the plan in question is a SIMPLE 401(k), $17,000 governs, not $24,500.
6. A plan document may impose a lower limit than the statutory one (for example, a percentage-of-pay cap), and nondiscrimination testing (ADP/ACP) may further constrain highly compensated employees. $24,500 is the statutory ceiling, not a guarantee of plan-level capacity.
7. Deferrals exceeding $24,500 for the year are includible in the employee's gross income and are correctable as excess deferrals under the plan's correction procedures; the participant, not only the plan administrator, is responsible for monitoring the aggregate across plans.

RELATED 2026 FIGURES ANNOUNCED IN THE SAME NOTICE (for cross-reference, not part of the answer)

- §415(c) annual additions limit: $72,000
- §415(b) defined benefit annual benefit limit: $290,000
- §401(a)(17) compensation limit: $360,000
- §402(g) elective deferral limit: $24,500 (the answer)
- §457(e)(15) deferred compensation deferral limit: $24,500
- Catch-up, age 50+: $8,000; ages 60–63: $11,250
- SIMPLE plan deferral limit: $17,000; SIMPLE catch-up: $4,000; SIMPLE ages 60–63 catch-up: $5,250

quotes.whole:
§ 50.18 National primary ambient air quality standards for PM2.5.




(a) The national primary ambient air quality standards for PM2.5 are 12.0 micrograms per cubic meter (µg/m3) annual arithmetic mean concentration and 35 µg/m3 24-hour average concentration measured in the ambient air as PM2.5 (particles with an aerodynamic diameter less than or equal to a nominal 2.5 micrometers) by either:




(1) A reference method based on appendix L to this part and designated in accordance with part 53 of this chapter; or






(2) An equivalent method designated in accordance with part 53 of this chapter.








(b) The primary annual PM2.5 standard is met when the annual arithmetic mean concentration, as determined in accordance with appendix N of this part, is less than or equal to 12.0 µg/m3.





(c) The primary 24-hour PM2.5 standard is met when the 98th percentile 24-hour concentration, as determined in accordance with appendix N of this part, is less than or equal to 35 µg/m3.

verdict.summary:
# Current US National Primary Ambient Air Quality Standards for PM2.5

## 1. Answer (the two requested levels)

| # | Standard | Level | Averaging time / form | Codification |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Primary **annual** PM2.5 | **9.0 µg/m³** | Annual arithmetic mean concentration; standard is met when the 3-year average of annual arithmetic means is ≤ 9.0 µg/m³ (40 CFR 50.20(b), App. N) | 40 CFR 50.20(a),(b); 89 FR 16380 (Mar. 6, 2024) |
| 2 | Primary **24-hour** PM2.5 | **35 µg/m³** | 24-hour average concentration; standard is met when the 3-year average of the annual 98th percentile 24-hour concentrations is ≤ 35 µg/m³ (40 CFR 50.20(c), App. N) | 40 CFR 50.20(a),(c); 89 FR 16380 (Mar. 6, 2024) |

Primary = health-based standards only, as requested. Both are measured in the ambient air as PM2.5 (particles with an aerodynamic diameter ≤ a nominal 2.5 µm) by an appendix L reference method or an equivalent method designated under part 53.

Effective date of the current annual level: **May 6, 2024** (final rule signed Feb. 7, 2024; published Mar. 6, 2024 at 89 FR 16380; effective 60 days later).

## 2. What the 2024 revision changed — and what it did not

- **Annual primary: 12.0 → 9.0 µg/m³.** This is the only level changed by the 2024 review.
- **24-hour primary: unchanged at 35 µg/m³.**
- **Secondary (welfare) PM2.5 standards: unchanged** at 15.0 µg/m³ annual and 35 µg/m³ 24-hour (reported here only for completeness; not part of the answer).
- The PM2.5 NAAQS were **recodified from 40 CFR 50.18 to 40 CFR 50.20** in the 2024 rule; §50.19 is the ozone NAAQS.

Historical note for anyone applying these levels to older data: for design values and attainment determinations based on monitoring years governed by the pre-2024 standards, the applicable annual level was **12.0 µg/m³** (78 FR 3277, Jan. 15, 2013). 12.0 is **superseded** and is not the current annual standard.

## 3. Rounding conventions (required to apply the levels correctly)

- **Annual:** the 3-year average of annual arithmetic means is rounded to the nearest 1 µg/m³ (decimals of 0.5 and greater round up) before comparison with 9.0 µg/m³.
- **24-hour:** the 3-year average of the annual 98th percentile 24-hour values is rounded to the nearest 1 µg/m³ before comparison with 35 µg/m³.
- Both are computed per 40 CFR part 50, appendix N.

## 4. How the apparent conflict in the source material was resolved (audit trail)

Two incompatible codifications appeared in the grounding:

1. An eCFR retrieval of §50.18 (fetched 2026-11-16T06:58:11Z, sha256 `7cf2e727c2ee`) showing **12.0 / 35** with citation [78 FR 3277, Jan. 15, 2013].
2. The CFR annual editions — 2024 (sha256 `f783e78d53f5`) and 2025 (printed 27 Jan 2026, sha256 `2a850915e78b`) — showing **§50.20** with **9.0 / 35** and citation [89 FR 16380, Mar. 6, 2024].

Discriminating evidence: the eCFR §50.18 text is **byte-for-byte identical** to the 2016 CFR XML (sha256 `d417980a789a`) and to the 2022 print, carrying the same 2013 Federal Register citation and no 2024 amendment. That is the signature of a **stale cached rendering**, not of a current codification — a currently-effective §50.18 containing the pre-2024 text would have to show a Federal Register action removing the 2024 amendment, and none exists in the record. The later-dated official annual edition (rev. July 1, 2025; printed Jan. 27, 2026) is therefore controlling: **§50.20, 9.0 µg/m³ annual / 35 µg/m³ 24-hour.**

## 5. Regulatory status caveats

- The 2024 PM2.5 rule was petitioned for review and remains the subject of litigation and of announced EPA reconsideration activity; it has **not been stayed or vacated**, and it remains codified. The levels above are the standards in force as of this response.
- "Current" is time-dependent: the annual level is the parameter that moves in EPA's periodic reviews (it has been 15.0, then 12.0, now 9.0 µg/m³). The 24-hour level has been 35 µg/m³ since the 2006/2012 reviews and is the more stable of the two.
- Anyone reusing this answer should re-confirm the annual figure against eCFR §50.20 at the time of use; if a future final rule revises it, only the annual entry changes.

## 6. Bottom line

The current US national primary ambient air quality standards for PM2.5 are **9.0 µg/m³, annual arithmetic mean** (3-year average of annual means, ≤ 9.0 µg/m³) and **35 µg/m³, 24-hour average** (3-year average of the annual 98th percentile, ≤ 35 µg/m³), codified at 40 CFR 50.20.

quotes.whole:
Toeboard means a low protective barrier that is designed to prevent materials, tools, and equipment from falling to a lower level, and protect employees from falling.
Travel restraint system means a combination of an anchorage, anchorage connector, lanyard (or other means of connection), and body support that an employer uses to eliminate the possibility of an employee going over the edge of a walking-working surface.
Tread means a horizontal member of a stair or stairway, but does not include landings or platforms.
Unprotected sides and edges mean any side or edge of a walking-working surface (except at entrances and other points of access) where there is no wall, guardrail system, or stair rail system to protect an employee from falling to a lower level.
Walking-working surface means any horizontal or vertical surface on or through which an employee walks, works, or gains access to a work area or workplace location.
Warning line means a barrier erected to warn employees that they are approaching an unprotected side or edge, and which designates an area in which work may take place without the use of other means of fall protection.

verdict.summary:
# Fall Protection Trigger Height - General Industry Walking-Working Surfaces (US, OSHA)

## 1. Answer

**4 feet (1.2 m).** A US employer covered by OSHA general industry standards must protect an employee on a walking-working surface that has an unprotected side or edge when the surface is **4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level**.

Controlling requirement: **29 CFR 1910.28(b)(1)(i)** (Unprotected sides and edges).

Directly-sourced corroboration from 29 CFR 1910.28(b)(15) ('Walking-working surfaces not otherwise addressed'): 'Except as provided elsewhere in this section or by other subparts of this part, the employer must ensure each employee on a walking-working surface 4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level is protected from falling by: (i) Guardrail systems; (ii) Safety net systems; or (iii) Personal fall protection systems, such as personal fall arrest, travel restraint, or positioning systems.'

Every specific paragraph in 1910.28(b) that addresses an unprotected edge uses the same 4 ft (1.2 m) trigger: stairway landings (b)(11)(i), rope descent systems (b)(12)(ii), slaughtering facility platforms (b)(14)(i), openings (b)(7), and dangerous equipment (b)(6)(ii). The 4 ft figure is the consistent general-industry baseline.

**Not the answer, but routinely confused with it:** construction work (29 CFR 1926 Subpart M) uses **6 feet (1.8 m)** under 1926.501(b)(1). That threshold does not apply to general industry walking-working surfaces.

## 2. Scope and how the threshold is measured

- **Applies to:** general industry employers under 29 CFR 1910 Subpart D (Walking-Working Surfaces), 1910.28(a).
- **Applies to:** any 'walking-working surface' - any horizontal or vertical surface on or through which an employee walks, works, or gains access to a work area or workplace location (1910.21(b)).
- **'Unprotected side or edge'** means any side or edge of a walking-working surface (except at entrances and other points of access) where there is no wall, guardrail system, or stair rail system to protect an employee from falling to a lower level (1910.21(b)). A parapet, wall, or existing guardrail/stair rail of adequate height means the side is not 'unprotected' and the duty is not triggered by that edge.
- **Measured vertically** from the walking-working surface on which the employee stands to the next lower level. Horizontal distance from the edge is irrelevant to the 4 ft trigger for general surfaces (it becomes relevant only for low-slope roofs, see section 5).
- **Inclusive threshold:** the duty attaches at exactly 4 ft 0 in and above ('4 feet or more'). There is no de minimis tolerance. 4 ft = 1.2192 m, which the regulation rounds to 1.2 m; a surface at 1.2 m satisfies the threshold under either unit.
- **Below 4 ft:** 1910.28(b)(1) does not require fall protection, but other provisions can still apply at lower heights - most importantly 1910.28(b)(6)(i), which requires a guardrail system or travel restraint system (unless the equipment is covered or guarded to eliminate the hazard) for an employee **less than** 4 ft above dangerous equipment.

## 3. What satisfies the duty

The employer must provide one or more of the following, installed and maintained per 1910.29:

1. **Guardrail system** - top rail 42 in (107 cm) +/- 3 in above the walking-working surface, midrail at approximately 21 in, capable of withstanding, without failure, a force of at least 200 lb (890 N) applied within 2 in of the top edge in any outward or downward direction.
2. **Safety net system** - installed as close as practicable under the surface, tested/rated per 1910.29(c).
3. **Personal fall arrest system (PFAS)** - per 1910.140: full-body harness, anchorage capable of supporting at least 5,000 lb (22.2 kN) per employee attached (or designed and installed under supervision of a qualified person as part of a complete PFAS maintaining a safety factor of at least two), and limited to a maximum free fall of 6 ft (1.8 m).
4. **Travel restraint system** - eliminates the possibility of the employee going over the edge; does not require a 5,000 lb anchorage but must be designed so the employee cannot reach the edge.
5. **Positioning system** - per 1910.140.
6. **Ladder safety system** - where the surface/access is a fixed ladder within 1910.28(b)(9).

Criteria above are 1910.29/1910.140 dimensions and strengths - they are not alternative trigger heights. The trigger height is always 4 ft (1.2 m) for a general walking-working surface.

## 4. No general 'infeasibility' escape on general surfaces

1910.28(b)(1) contains no general infeasibility or greater-hazard exemption for ordinary walking-working surfaces. Unlike construction (1926.501(b)(2) and the 1926.502(k) fall protection plan), a general-industry employer cannot simply declare guardrails infeasible and omit protection on a 4 ft-plus platform. Where the standard permits an alternative, it says so expressly and narrowly - e.g., 1910.28(b)(14)(ii) for slaughtering facility platforms (work operation in process, access limited to authorized employees, employees trained per 1910.30), and 1910.28(b)(13)(iii) for work far from a low-slope roof edge. Any reliance on such a provision must track its exact conditions.

## 5. Provisions that displace or duplicate the 4 ft trigger (all values as stated in the standard)

| Provision | Situation | Trigger / value |
|---|---|---|
| 1910.28(b)(1) | General walking-working surface, unprotected side or edge | **4 ft (1.2 m)** |
| 1910.28(b)(6)(i) | Employee **less than** 4 ft above dangerous equipment | Guardrail or travel restraint required regardless (unless equipment covered/guarded) |
| 1910.28(b)(6)(ii) | Employee **4 ft or more** above dangerous equipment | Guardrail, safety net, travel restraint, or PFAS |
| 1910.28(b)(7) | Opening with inside bottom edge < 39 in (99 cm) and outside bottom edge >= 4 ft (1.2 m) | Guardrail, safety net, travel restraint, or PFAS |
| 1910.28(b)(11)(i) | Stairway landing with unprotected side or edge | 4 ft (1.2 m) - guardrail or stair rail system |
| 1910.28(b)(12)(ii) | Rope descent system | 4 ft (1.2 m) - PFAS |
| 1910.28(b)(12)(i) | Scaffolds | Governed by 29 CFR 1926 Subpart L (scaffold fall protection attaches above 10 ft / 3.05 m under 1926.451(g)(1)) |
| 1910.28(b)(13)(i) | Low-slope roof, work **less than 6 ft** from edge | Guardrail, safety net, travel restraint, or PFAS (no height trigger - the roof-edge distance governs) |
| 1910.28(b)(13)(ii) | Low-slope roof, work **6 ft to < 15 ft** from edge | Same systems; designated area allowed if work is infrequent and temporary |
| 1910.28(b)(13)(iii) | Low-slope roof, work **15 ft or more** from edge | Guardrail/net/travel restraint/PFAS or designated area; no fall protection required if work is both infrequent and temporary, plus a work rule prohibiting employees within 15 ft of the edge without protection |
| 1910.28(b)(14)(i) | Slaughtering facility platform, unprotected working side | 4 ft (1.2 m) - guardrail or travel restraint |
| 1910.28(b)(9) | Fixed ladders | Separate 24 ft (7.3 m) trigger for ladder safety system / PFAS, with cage-and-well phase-out; **verify current text before relying on this row** |
| 1926.501(b)(1) | Construction (contrast only) | 6 ft (1.8 m) |

Note on roofs: 1910.28(b)(1) begins 'Except as provided elsewhere in this section,' so 1910.28(b)(13) controls low-slope roof work. A worker on a roof 20 ft above grade who is 15 ft or more from the edge, performing infrequent and temporary work under an enforced 15 ft work rule, is not required to have fall protection - the 4 ft drop does not by itself create a duty in that specific case. This is the principal situation in which the 4 ft baseline yields.

## 6. Compliance / audit procedure (apply directly)

1. **Inventory** every walking-working surface employees use: platforms, mezzanines, catwalks, roofs, pits, tank tops, loading docks, equipment tops.
2. **Measure** the vertical drop from the working surface to the next lower level for each exposed edge. Record the dimension in feet and metres to two decimals (e.g., 3.83 ft / 1.17 m).
3. **Classify** each edge as protected or unprotected using the 1910.21(b) definition: is there a wall, guardrail system, or stair rail system? A 30 in parapet is not a compliant guardrail (top rail must be 42 in +/- 3 in) - treat the edge as unprotected and the 4 ft duty as triggered.
4. **Apply the trigger:** drop >= 4 ft 0 in (1.2 m) and edge unprotected -> fall protection required. Drop < 4 ft -> check 1910.28(b)(6) (dangerous equipment) and any other applicable paragraph before concluding no protection is needed.
5. **Check precedence:** confirm no other paragraph of 1910.28(b) or other subpart governs the specific surface (roof, scaffold, ladder, rope descent, slaughtering platform). Document which provision controls.
6. **Select and verify the system** against 1910.29 / 1910.140 criteria (guardrail 42 in +/- 3 in top rail, 21 in midrail, 200 lb / 890 N load; PFAS anchorage 5,000 lb / 22.2 kN per employee or qualified-person design with safety factor >= 2; maximum free fall 6 ft / 1.8 m).
7. **Train** affected employees per 1910.30 (nature of hazards, correct use, inspection, limitations, rescue) and **document** the hazard assessment, the selected system, and the training records.
8. **Re-evaluate** after any change in process, equipment, or layout, and after any incident or near miss.

## 7. Jurisdiction note

Federal OSHA sets 4 ft (1.2 m) for general industry. OSHA-approved State Plans must be at least as effective as federal OSHA and may adopt more stringent or additional requirements (for example, stricter trigger heights, guardrail dimensions, or training rules). Where the workplace is in a State Plan state, verify the state's general-industry walking-working surfaces rule before finalizing the protection height.

## 8. Self-check of every number used in this answer

- 4 ft = 1.2192 m; regulation states 1.2 m. Consistent.
- 4 ft threshold is inclusive; 3 ft 11 in falls below it and does not trigger (b)(1). Consistent with (b)(6)(i), which covers the sub-4-ft case for dangerous equipment.
- Guardrail top rail 42 in (3.5 ft) < 48 in (4 ft): a dimensional criterion, not a competing trigger. Consistent.
- Midrail 21 in < 42 in top rail. Consistent.
- Opening inside bottom edge 39 in (3.25 ft) < 48 in. Consistent.
- PFAS free fall 6 ft and anchorage 5,000 lb are criteria, not trigger heights. Consistent.
- Scaffold 10 ft (1926 Subpart L) > 4 ft; construction 6 ft > 4 ft; fixed ladder 24 ft > 4 ft. All higher than or separate from the general-industry 4 ft baseline, so none contradicts the stated answer.
- Roof distances 6 ft and 15 ft are horizontal distances from the roof edge, a different axis than the 4 ft vertical drop; the roof provision displaces (b)(1) by its own terms. Consistent.

## 9. Common errors to avoid

- Quoting 6 ft (the construction threshold) for a general-industry facility.
- Treating a parapet, toe board, or warning line as fall protection where 1910.28(b)(1) requires a guardrail, net, or personal fall protection system (warning lines/designated areas are permitted only where a specific paragraph allows them, e.g., low-slope roofs).
- Measuring horizontally from the edge instead of vertically to the lower level.
- Assuming a general infeasibility exemption exists for general walking-working surfaces.
- Overlooking 1910.28(b)(6) for drops under 4 ft onto dangerous equipment.

verdict.summary:
# VFR Reserve Fuel for a Helicopter in the United States

## Answer

**20 minutes.** A helicopter (rotorcraft) may not begin a VFR flight in the US unless it carries enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing **and then fly for at least 20 minutes** at normal cruising speed / normal cruising fuel consumption.

The 20-minute reserve is the same **day or night**, and it is the same under **Part 91** and **Part 135**. There is no 30/45-minute day/night split for helicopters — that split applies to airplanes only.

## Regulatory basis

**14 CFR § 91.151(b) — Fuel requirements for flight in VFR conditions (Part 91):**

> "No person may begin a flight in a rotorcraft under VFR conditions unless (considering wind and forecast weather conditions) there is enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and, assuming normal cruising speed, to fly after that for at least 20 minutes."

**14 CFR § 135.209(b) — VFR: Fuel supply (Part 135):**

> "No person may begin a flight operation in a helicopter under VFR unless, considering wind and forecast weather conditions, it has enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and, assuming normal cruising fuel consumption, to fly after that for at least 20 minutes."

Note the wording difference only: Part 91 says "normal cruising **speed**," Part 135 says "normal cruising **fuel consumption**." The required reserve time is identical at 20 minutes.

## Comparison table (to prevent misapplication)

| Operation | Rule | Reserve after first point of intended landing |
|---|---|---|
| **Helicopter / rotorcraft, VFR, day** | 91.151(b) / 135.209(b) | **20 minutes** |
| **Helicopter / rotorcraft, VFR, night** | 91.151(b) / 135.209(b) | **20 minutes** (no change) |
| Airplane, VFR, day | 91.151(a)(1) / 135.209(a)(1) | 30 minutes |
| Airplane, VFR, night | 91.151(a)(2) / 135.209(a)(2) | 45 minutes |
| Helicopter, IFR (after alternate, if required) | 91.167(a)(3) | 30 minutes (IFR — not applicable to a VFR flight) |

Only the first two rows answer this question. The airplane rows and the IFR row are shown so the 20-minute figure is not confused with them; none of them is an alternative VFR helicopter reserve.

## Converting 20 minutes to a fuel quantity

Because the rule is stated in time, the reserve must be converted using the helicopter's own normal cruising fuel burn:

```
Reserve fuel (gal) = (20 / 60) x normal cruise burn (gal/hr)
                   = normal cruise burn (gal/hr) / 3
```

Representative conversions (illustrative only — use the actual aircraft's cruise burn from its performance data):

| Normal cruise burn | 20-min reserve |
|---|---|
| 8 gal/hr | 2.7 gal |
| 12 gal/hr | 4.0 gal |
| 15 gal/hr | 5.0 gal |
| 20 gal/hr | 6.7 gal |
| 30 gal/hr | 10.0 gal |

## Worked example (full fuel plan)

Given: cruise 30 gal/hr, trip time to first point of intended landing 1.5 hr, unusable fuel 1.5 gal.

```
Trip fuel      = 1.5 hr x 30 gal/hr        = 45.0 gal
VFR reserve    = 20 min = 0.333 hr x 30    = 10.0 gal
Subtotal (usable fuel required)            = 55.0 gal
Unusable fuel (must be on board but not burnable) = 1.5 gal
Minimum fuel on board at start             = 56.5 gal
```

The 10.0 gal reserve is exactly one-third of the hourly burn, consistent with the 20-minute rule; no other reserve figure appears in this plan.

## Conditions built into the rule (apply them, don't skip them)

1. **"Considering wind and forecast weather conditions"** — the trip fuel and the reserve are both computed against forecast winds and temperatures, not still-air book figures. A headwind on the return leg can make the 20 minutes represent fewer miles than expected; the rule requires the *time*, so the fuel must be sufficient for 20 minutes of actual cruise in the conditions forecast.
2. **"Normal cruising speed" / "normal cruising fuel consumption"** — the reserve is computed at the helicopter's normal cruise power setting, not at a max-range or loiter setting chosen to shrink the number.
3. **"To begin a flight"** — compliance is measured at the moment of takeoff. A flight that launches legal but arrives with less than 20 minutes remaining because of unforecast winds has still met the rule only if the forecast was properly considered; in practice, plan so the reserve survives a plausible deviation.
4. **No alternate-airport fuel requirement in VFR** — the 91.167/135.219 alternate fuel and weather rules are IFR rules and do not add to this VFR reserve. For a VFR helicopter flight, the requirement is trip fuel plus 20 minutes.
5. **Usable vs. total fuel** — the 20 minutes must be burnable. Unusable fuel and fuel that cannot be accessed in the aircraft's attitude/configuration do not count toward the reserve; add them on top, as in the worked example.

## What the 20 minutes is and is not

- It **is** the regulatory floor. It is the minimum a pilot must have on board to launch legally under Part 91 or Part 135.
- It **is not** a planning target. Operators commonly impose higher reserves (company fuel policy, OpSpecs, insurance or lease requirements, offshore/oil-and-gas contracts, HEMS programs). Those can be, and often are, 30 minutes or more. The regulation sets the floor, not the ceiling.
- It **is not** affected by day/night for helicopters. A night VFR helicopter flight still requires 20 minutes, not 45.
- It **is not** the IFR helicopter reserve (30 minutes after the alternate, per 91.167(a)(3)); that rule does not govern a VFR flight.

## One-line answer

A helicopter beginning a VFR flight in the US must carry fuel to reach the first point of intended landing plus **20 minutes** of additional flying at normal cruising speed — 14 CFR 91.151(b) for Part 91 operations and 14 CFR 135.209(b) for Part 135 operations, with no day/night difference for rotorcraft.

quotes.whole:
Abstract
This document formally deprecates Transport Layer
Security (TLS) versions 1.0 (RFC 2246) and 1.1 (RFC 4346).
Accordingly, those documents have been moved
to Historic status. These versions lack support for current
and recommended cryptographic algorithms and mechanisms, and
various government and industry profiles of applications using
TLS now mandate avoiding these old TLS versions. TLS version 1.2
became the recommended version for IETF protocols in 2008
(subsequently being obsoleted by TLS version 1.3 in 2018), providing
sufficient time to transition away from older versions.
Removing support for older versions from implementations reduces the
attack surface, reduces opportunity for misconfiguration, and
streamlines library and product maintenance.¶
This document also deprecates Datagram TLS (DTLS) version 1.0
(RFC 4347) but not DTLS version 1.2, and there is no DTLS
version 1.1.¶
This document updates many RFCs that normatively refer to TLS version 1.0 or
TLS version 1.1, as described herein. This document also updates the best
practices for TLS usage in RFC 7525; hence, it is part of BCP 195.¶
Status of This Memo
This memo documents an Internet Best Current Practice.¶

Deprecating TLSv1.0 and TLSv1.1
draft-ietf-tls-oldversions-deprecate-12
Abstract
This document, if approved, formally deprecates Transport Layer
Security (TLS) versions 1.0 (RFC 2246) and 1.1 (RFC 4346).
Accordingly, those documents (will be moved|have been moved) to
Historic status.  These versions lack support for current and
recommended cryptographic algorithms and mechanisms, and various
government and industry profiles of applications using TLS now
mandate avoiding these old TLS versions.  TLSv1.2 became the
recommended version for IETF protocols in 2008, (subsequently being
obsoleted by TLSv1.3 in 2018), providing sufficient time to
transition away from older versions.  Removing support for older
versions from implementations reduces the attack surface, reduces
opportunity for misconfiguration, and streamlines library and product
maintenance.
This document also deprecates Datagram TLS (DTLS) version 1.0 (RFC
4347), but not DTLS version 1.2, and there is no DTLS version 1.1.
This document updates many RFCs that normatively refer to TLSv1.0 or
TLSv1.1 as described herein.  This document also updates the best
practices for TLS usage in RFC 7525 and hence is part of BCP 195.

1.  Introduction
Transport Layer Security (TLS) versions 1.0 [RFC2246] and 1.1
[RFC4346] were superseded by TLSv1.2 [RFC5246] in 2008, which has now
itself been superseded by TLSv1.3 [RFC8446].  Datagram Transport
Layer Security (DTLS) version 1.0 [RFC4347] was superseded by
DTLSv1.2 [RFC6347] in 2012.  It is therefore timely to further
deprecate TLSv1.0, TLSv1.1 and DTLSv1.0.  Accordingly, those
documents (will be moved|have been moved) to Historic status.
Technical reasons for deprecating these versions include:
o  They require implementation of older cipher suites that are no
longer desirable for cryptographic reasons, e.g., TLSv1.0 makes
TLS_DHE_DSS_WITH_3DES_EDE_CBC_SHA mandatory to implement
o  Lack of support for current recommended cipher suites, especially
AEAD ciphers which are not supported prior to TLSv1.2.  Note:
registry entries for no-longer-desirable ciphersuites remain in
the registries, but many TLS registries are being updated through
[RFC8447] which indicates that such entries are not recommended by
the IETF.
o  Integrity of the handshake depends on SHA-1 hash.
o  Authentication of the peers depends on SHA-1 signatures.

verdict.summary:
## Answer

**1. The RFC that deprecated TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 is RFC 8996**, "Deprecating TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1" (March 2021), part of BCP 195.

**2. The status it gave to the RFCs that defined those versions is Historic.** Specifically, RFC 2246 (TLS 1.0) and RFC 4346 (TLS 1.1) were moved to Historic status.

## Evidence from the primary source

From the abstract of RFC 8996 (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8996.html):

> "This document formally deprecates Transport Layer Security (TLS) versions 1.0 (RFC 2246) and 1.1 (RFC 4346). Accordingly, those documents have been moved to Historic status."

From Section 1 (Introduction) of the same document:

> "Transport Layer Security (TLS) versions 1.0 [RFC2246] and 1.1 [RFC4346] were superseded by TLS 1.2 [RFC5246] in 2008, which has now itself been superseded by TLS 1.3 [RFC8446]. ... Therefore, it is timely to further deprecate TLS 1.0, TLS 1.1, and DTLS 1.0. Accordingly, the aforementioned documents have been moved to Historic status."

The document title and number are confirmed by the RFC Editor info page and the IETF Datatracker history page, which lists "RFC 8996 (2021-03-23)" with the title "Deprecating TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1".

## Disambiguation (important, to avoid a misreading)

Two different "statuses" are in play and should not be conflated:

| Subject | Status |
|---|---|
| RFC 8996 itself (the deprecating document) | Internet Best Current Practice (part of BCP 195) — per its "Status of This Memo": "This memo documents an Internet Best Current Practice." |
| RFC 2246 (TLS 1.0) and RFC 4346 (TLS 1.1) — the RFCs that defined the deprecated versions | **Historic** — this is the answer to ask 2 |

So the answer to "what status did it give the RFCs that had defined them" is **Historic**, not "Best Current Practice" (that is RFC 8996's own status).

## Scope note (context, not part of the answer)

RFC 8996's deprecation is not limited to TLS 1.0 and 1.1. The same document also deprecates DTLS 1.0 (RFC 4347), leaves DTLS 1.2 alone ("there is no DTLS version 1.1"), moves RFC 5469 to Historic, marks RFC 7507's fallback SCSV functionality as superseded, and updates many RFCs that normatively reference TLS 1.0 or 1.1 — including an update to RFC 7525, which is why it is part of BCP 195. The two protocol-defining RFCs named in the question, however, are exactly RFC 2246 and RFC 4346, and both were assigned Historic.

## One-line result

RFC 8996 deprecated TLS 1.0 (RFC 2246) and TLS 1.1 (RFC 4346), and moved both of those defining RFCs to **Historic** status.

Social Security's Old-Age, Survivors, and Disability
Insurance (OASDI) program limits the amount of earnings subject to taxation for
a given year.  The same annual limit also applies when those earnings are used
in a benefit computation.  This limit changes each year with changes
in the national average wage index.  We call this annual
limit the contribution and benefit base.  This amount is also commonly referred
to as the taxable maximum. For earnings in 2027, this base is
$192,300.
The OASDI tax rate for wages paid in
2027 is set by statute at 6.2 percent for employees and employers, each. Thus,
an individual with wages equal to or larger than $192,300 would contribute $11,922.60
to the OASDI program in 2027, and his or her employer would contribute the same
amount. The OASDI tax rate for self-employment income in 2027 is 12.4 percent.

Contribution and Benefit Base Determination
Automatic Determinations
Contribution & Benefit Base
Wage-indexed Amounts
Method for determining the base
The formula for determining the OASDI contribution and benefit base
is set by law. The formula is applicable only if a
cost-of-living increase becomes
effective for December of the year in which a determination of
the base would ordinarily be made.  Because there is a cost-of-living increase for December 2026, the
formula is applicable.  The formula states that the base for any year
Y after 1994 is equal to the 1994 base of $60,600 multiplied by
the ratio of the national average wage index for
year (Y-2) to that for 1992, with the result rounded to the nearest
multiple of $300.  If the result is less than the current base, the base
is not reduced.
Base for 2027
Under the above formula, the base for 2027 shall be the 1994 base of $60,600
multiplied by the ratio of the national average wage index for 2025 to that for
1992, or, if larger, the 2026 base of $184,500.  If the amount so determined
is not a multiple of $300, it is rounded to the nearest multiple of $300.

The Long-Run Financial Outlook
Social Security is not sustainable over the long term at current benefit and tax rates. Since 2010, the program has annually paid more in benefits and expenses than it collected in taxes and other noninterest income, and the 2026 Trustees Report projects this pattern to continue for the next 75 years. The Trustees estimate that the combined OASI and DI trust fund reserves will be depleted by 2034. At that point, payroll taxes and other income will flow into the fund but will be sufficient to pay only about 83% of program costs. As reported in the 2026 Trustees Report, the projected shortfall over the next 75 years is 4.24% of taxable payroll.

verdict.summary:
# US Social Security contribution and benefit base (taxable maximum) for 2026

## Answer

**$184,500** — the maximum amount of earnings subject to the Social Security (OASDI) payroll tax for wages paid in calendar year 2026, and the same limit used in benefit computations for that year. This is the official, final, announced figure, not a projection.

## Sources (all Social Security Administration, primary)

| Source | What it states |
|---|---|
| SSA, *Contribution and Benefit Base* (ssa.gov/oact/COLA/cbb.html) | Year table: 2025 = $176,100; **2026 = $184,500**; 2027 = $192,300 |
| SSA, *Fast Facts & Figures About Social Security, 2026* (ssa.gov/policy/docs/chartbooks/fast_facts/2026/fast_facts26.html) | 'Maximum earnings subject to Social Security taxes, 2026': OASDI = **184,500**; HI = No limit |
| SSA, *Contribution and Benefit Base Determination* (ssa.gov/oact/COLA/cbbdet.html) | Refers to 'the 2026 base of $184,500' as the current base in the 2027 determination |

Three independent SSA pages agree; no discrepancy to resolve.

## How the figure is set (statutory method)

Under the automatic-adjustment provisions of the Social Security Act, the base for year Y after 1994 is:

    base(Y) = $60,600 x [ AWI(Y-2) / AWI(1992) ] , rounded to the nearest multiple of $300

where AWI is the national average wage index and $60,600 is the 1994 base. Two conditions apply:

- The formula operates only if a cost-of-living increase is effective for December of the preceding year.
- The base is never reduced below the prior year's base.

Checks against those rules for 2026: $184,500 is an exact multiple of $300 (184,500 / 300 = 615), as the rounding rule requires, and it exceeds the 2025 base of $176,100, so the no-decrease floor is not triggered. (The grounding does not include the 2024 AWI value used in the 2026 computation, so no numeric back-solution is asserted here; the fully sourced worked example the SSA publishes is the 2027 one: $60,600 x 72,800.33 / 22,935.42 = $192,353.14 → $192,300.)

## Derived amounts on the 2026 base (for reference)

| Item | Rate | Amount |
|---|---|---|
| Employee OASDI tax at the base | 6.2% | $11,439.00 |
| Employer OASDI tax at the base | 6.2% | $11,439.00 |
| Combined employee + employer | 12.4% | $22,878.00 |
| Self-employed OASDI tax at the base | 12.4% | $22,878.00 |

These apply only up to $184,500 of covered earnings; they exclude the Medicare HI tax, which has no earnings cap.

## Bounderies and common confusions

- **Medicare (HI) has no wage base.** Per Fast Facts 2026, the HI 'maximum' is 'No limit'; the OASDI cap applies only to Social Security. Do not report $184,500 as a Medicare cap.
- **Year-specific.** $184,500 is the 2026 figure. The adjacent values are $176,100 (2025) and $192,300 (2027, already announced). The 2027 announcement does not change the 2026 amount.
- **Not the same as other wage-indexed parameters.** The base is distinct from the retirement earnings-test exempt amounts, the benefit-formula bend points, the maximum monthly benefit ($4,152 for workers retiring at full retirement age in 2026), and the work-credit threshold ($1,890 per credit; $7,560 for four credits in 2026).
- **Wages vs. self-employment.** For an employee with multiple jobs, excess employee tax withheld above the base is refundable; employers cannot claim that refund. For the self-employed, covered net earnings are taxable up to the base, reduced by any taxable wages already counted against it.

## Caveats

- The figure is stated in nominal US dollars, whole dollars, for calendar year 2026; no rounding or currency conversion was applied.
- Source pages were retrieved 2026-11-16, at which point both the 2026 and 2027 determinations were published; the 2026 amount is therefore final and not subject to revision.

WASHINGTON — The Internal Revenue Service announced today that the amount individuals can contribute to their 401(k) plans in 2026 has increased to $24,500, up from $23,500 for 2025.
The IRS today also issued technical guidance regarding all cost‑of‑living adjustments affecting dollar limitations for pension plans and other retirement-related items for tax year 2026 in Notice 2025-67 PDF, posted today on IRS.gov.
Highlights of changes for 2026
The annual contribution limit for employees who participate in 401(k), 403(b), governmental 457 plans, and the federal government’s Thrift Savings Plan is increased to $24,500, up from $23,500 for 2025.
The limit on annual contributions to an IRA is increased to $7,500 from $7,000. The IRA catch‑up contribution limit for individuals aged 50 and over was amended under the SECURE 2.0 Act of 2022 (SECURE 2.0) to include an annual cost‑of‑living adjustment is increased to $1,100, up from $1,000 for 2025.

Taxpayers can deduct contributions to a traditional IRA if they meet certain conditions. If during the year either the taxpayer or the taxpayer’s spouse was covered by a retirement plan at work, the deduction may be reduced, or phased out, until it is eliminated, depending on filing status and income. (If neither the taxpayer nor the spouse is covered by a retirement plan at work, the phase-outs of the deduction do not apply.) Here are the phase‑out ranges for 2026:
For single taxpayers covered by a workplace retirement plan, the phase-out range is increased to between $81,000 and $91,000, up from between $79,000 and $89,000 for 2025.
For married couples filing jointly, if the spouse making the IRA contribution is covered by a workplace retirement plan, the phase-out range is increased to between $129,000 and $149,000, up from between $126,000 and $146,000 for 2025.
For an IRA contributor who is not covered by a workplace retirement plan and is married to someone who is covered, the phase-out range is increased to between $242,000 and $252,000, up from between $236,000 and $246,000 for 2025.

verdict.summary:
ANSWER — 2026 elective deferral limit (401(k)), before catch-up

The limit on an employee's elective deferrals to a 401(k) plan for the 2026 calendar/tax year, before any catch-up contribution, is $24,500.

This is the IRC §402(g)(1) limitation on the exclusion for elective deferrals, as adjusted for cost of living. In statutory form the limit is the lesser of $24,500 or 100% of the employee's compensation; for any employee earning at least $24,500 the operative figure is $24,500.

AUTHORITY
- IRS Notice 2025-67 (2026 cost-of-living adjustments for pension and retirement items): the §402(g)(1) limitation 'is increased from $23,500 to $24,500.' The same notice increases the §457(e)(15) limit to $24,500.
- IRS News Release IR-2025-111 (Nov. 13, 2025): 'The annual contribution limit for employees who participate in 401(k), 403(b), governmental 457 plans, and the federal government's Thrift Savings Plan is increased to $24,500, up from $23,500 for 2025.'
- IRS Retirement Topics — 401(k) and Profit-Sharing Plan Contribution Limits: 'The limit on employee elective deferrals (for traditional and safe harbor plans) is: $24,500 in 2026, subject to cost-of-living adjustments.'
- IRS Publication 560: 'The limit on elective deferrals, other than catch-up contributions, is $23,500 for 2025 and $24,500 for 2026.'

WHAT THE $24,500 COVERS AND WHAT IT DOES NOT
- Counts against it: pre-tax (traditional) elective deferrals and designated Roth elective deferrals made to the 401(k) plan, plus elective deferrals to any other 401(k), 403(b), SARSEP, or governmental 457(b) plan of the same employer (or controlled group). The limit is applied to the aggregate, not per plan.
- Does not count against it: employer matching contributions, employer nonelective contributions, forfeiture allocations, and catch-up contributions. These are governed by the separate §415(c) annual additions limit ($72,000 for 2026, excluding catch-up).
- Does not include catch-up: an eligible participant age 50 or over may defer an additional $8,000 in 2026 (and $11,250 for participants who attain age 60, 61, 62, or 63 in 2026) if the plan permits, for a potential total of $32,500 (or $35,750 for the age 60-63 group). Those amounts are expressly outside the answer above and must not be added to the $24,500 figure when stating the pre-catch-up limit.

ADJACENT 2026 FIGURES — FOR DISAMBIGUATION ONLY (not the answer)
| Limit | 2026 amount |
|---|---|
| §402(g) elective deferral, 401(k)/403(b)/governmental 457(b)/SARSEP | $24,500 |
| Age-50 catch-up, non-SIMPLE plans | $8,000 |
| Age 60-63 catch-up, non-SIMPLE plans | $11,250 |
| SIMPLE 401(k) / SIMPLE IRA deferral limit | $17,000 |
| SIMPLE catch-up (age 50+) | $4,000 |
| §415(c) annual additions (DC plans, excl. catch-up) | $72,000 |
| §401(a)(17) compensation limit | $360,000 |

HR / PLAN-ADMINISTRATION NOTES
1. Plan document may be lower. A plan may impose a lower deferral cap than $24,500; the IRS limit is a ceiling, not an entitlement. Check the plan's adoption agreement/SPD before communicating the figure.
2. Nondiscrimination testing may reduce it further. Highly compensated employees may have deferrals limited by the ADP test (or refunded after year-end), even though $24,500 remains the statutory maximum.
3. Payroll setup. Configure the deferral source to stop at $24,500 in aggregate across the controlled group for 2026; excess deferrals must be corrected (distributed with attributable earnings by the applicable deadline, generally April 15 of the following year) and are includible in gross income in the year deferred.
4. Mid-year hires and multiple plans. Proration is not permitted; the full $24,500 applies regardless of hire date, but an employee participating in more than one plan of the same employer has one combined $24,500 limit.
5. Effective date. The figure is the IRS-announced 2026 amount, published November 13, 2025, and is not a projection or estimate.

Bottom line: $24,500 for 2026, before catch-up.
